My hon. friend says-and possibly he may be right from a legal standpoint- that the gates were down and that this woman went under ithe gates or around them; but the Minister of Railways must not forget that that crossing for years has been a menace to the lives of the people of the city of Moncton. Considering all ithe circumstances, I think it is a very strong case for the consideration of my hon. friend the Minister of Railways.
On what ground would you advise giving the compensation.
Compassionate allowance.

As suggested by the General Manager of the Intercolonial, some compassionate allowance should be given to Mr. O'Rourke. I am not standing here to-day as solicitor for the Intercolonial to advise the hon. Minister of Railways from a legal standpoint; but, speaking from my knowledge of the situation, I would say that, whatever compensation or compassionate allowance is given to Mr. O'Rourke by the Minister of Railways, no criticism nor objection will be offered by my constituents or by any hon. member in the House.

When the hon. member gets the further information for which he is waiting, I shall be very glad to discuss the matter with him; but it is a dangerous precedent to establish, to give compensation when a person deliberately goes on a railway line that is protected, and gets killed.
Intercolonial Railway-Amherst-Additional facilities, $16,000.
What has been done at Amherst?
Additional tracks necessary to provide for increased business at that point, as voted in 1914-15. The money was not expended last year.
What struck me is the fact that the money, though voted, had not been expended. Is the minister going to expend it this year ?
I hope so.
It seems a pity to vote it when we are so hard up if we do not intend to spend it.
I know; but if things improve we ought to have the money to expend. The improvements are absolutely necessary there for the accommodation of the traffic.
What action does the minister propose to take in regard to the construction of a bridge across Pictou harbour ? I understand the matter has been under investigation.

It is, but I am sorry to say the investigation has proved the work a difficult one. The mud is very deep. We have not come to a conclusion in reference to this work. I hope we shall come to a conclusion by next session, but we aTe not providing any money for it [DOT]this session.

I know it is not the minister's fault. The engineers he sent there last year to take the soundings, instead of working as they should have done on the ice, delayed and fooled along with the work, and did not get their soundings until after the ice had gone out, when the work could not be done with as great perfection as when the ice was there. There is grave local complaint among friends of the hon. gentleman as to the way the engineers dealt with the question.
This winter ?
No, last winter. This winter they were there only a day or two, and were said to be verifying some examination they had made before.
I will make a note of the matter.

I understand the
position to be that the minister does not intend to do anything in the way of construction this year?
No.

Another matter to
which I wish to refer is the case of Mrs.
Higgins, who was injured on the 23rd of August, 1914, at Ferrona station. I would ask the minister to have inquiry made. It is a case of the train starting too quickly before this old lady could alight. From the information given me there is great merit in the case, and it is desirable, where a railway is in fault, and cannot show negligence on the part of the person injured, that it should settle with the party.
I will take a note of it.

I understand the
minister to say with reference to the plans he has brought down, that the line of railway he proposes to construct would run from Sunnybrae through Guysborough county and the town of Guysborough to Mulgrave. The minister showned me the plan and stated that he proposed going by East River, St. Alary's. I think he is taking the right course. He will go through a settled country which is very fertile and where the conditions are very good, indeed. I have always contended for that route when my hon. friend the former Minister of Railways (Air. Graham) placed in the Estimates, as he did, a vote of $1,000,000 for the purpose of constructing that road. I pressed upon him in the strongest possible way the desirability of following this route which the present minister tells me he has adopted, going through the garden of Eden and East River, St. Mary's section. I hope that, now that he has come round to the policy of his predecessor in constructing this road, though there has been a delay of some three or four years in the adopting of it- he will go on with the construction of the railway.

To be fair, was there
not a little dispute then as to the way it should go? No definite route was decided upon, I think.

The whole was decided upon excepting with regard to the disputed point, for which I contended and which, as the minister will recall, I have frequently supported in the House since he became minister. Do I understand that the minister intends to proceed immediately to construct?
As soon as we can get ready.
What effect will this have upon the portion of the line from New Glasgow to Alulgrave?

There is a portion of that line which had a rather heavy track, coming up from the ferry, on which the grades will be better. Going east the grades will be .6 per cent, and going the other way, .5 per cent.
And what are the grades on the other line?
I have not the figures, but I think they run over 1 per cent.
So the minister expects they will be able to make better time?
No doubt about it. The hon. gentleman knows the state of the old road. With the improvements in the grades an engine will do nearly one-third more.
In spite of the additional distance?
It is only a short distance. This line is only 88 miles, and the hon. gentleman knows the distance over the other.
So that the minister anticipates that when this road is constructed it will be a great highway for the traffic coming through from Cape Breton.
I think it will be a great improvement on the present route.
If I understand the minister's proposition, the line from Sunnybrae to Port Mulgrave will be the main line of the Intercolonial railway?
I said it would carry heavy traffic; but we will have to maintain the other line.

The minister points out that, as the grades will be lighter on the new line, the heavy traffic will necessarily go over that line. The result will be that the present line from New Glasgow to Mulgrave running through Antigonish will be merely a side line and only local traffic will be done on it. Has the minister looked into the facts to ascertain whether or not the present line could be improved, the grades reduced and the railway generally straightened out to enable it to carry as heavy traffic as the proposed new line? Three years ago there was a petition from Harbour au Bouche asking that the line be diverted from Lin wood, running through Cape Jack and the village of Havre Boucher on to Mulgrave, instead of as now. This would get rid of the heavy grade

between Big Tracadie and Mulgrave. I suppose the minister will say now, as he has said on previous occasions, that he is not responsible for the assurances of alleged agents or Tory emissaries who claim to have authority from him, but I may say that assurances were given that this diversion was going to be made. I see now that the minister does not propose doing that; he proposes that the general traffic shall cease to be carried through the county of Antigonish-through the districts of Harbour au Bouche, Linwood, Tracadie, Pom-quet, Heatherton, South River, James River-and that the people shall be served by a mere side line. I am sure that this will be a great source of disappointment to the people of that district. I hope that before the minister commits himself to the policy which he proposes, he will look into the matter more carefully. Of course, I do not imagine that he is going on with the construction of this line just now; there are certain reasons, perhaps, why this item should appear in the Estimates.
Is it not a proper line to build?

I am quite in sympathy with the construction of the line through Guysborough county, but I am not in sympathy with the degrading of that portion of the road which runs through the county which *t have the honour to represent. the Conservative party are not living up to their pledges-that, of course, will surprise them-because instead of improving the road, as they promised to do; instead of furnishing better accommodations, assurance of which they gave the people of the eastern portion of Antigonish county, they are putting them off with a side line. Guysborough is the only county in the whole province that has not had railway accommodations. The Intercolonial railway runs through the northern part of Nova Scotia; in the southern part of the province there is the Halifax and Southwestern. After the' construction of the Halifax and Eastern line was got under way, every county in the province with the exception of Guysborough and possibly Victoria, had been provided with railway transportation facilities. I approve, therefore, of the building of a line through Guysborough county; with that proposal I find absolutely no fault, although I Jo not know whether the route proposed is the most feasible. What I do find fault with, however, is that the Government proposes to put the people in that section of the country to which

I have referred on a side line, and the result will be that that portion of the line will not receive the attention that it otherwise would receive.
What I did say was that probably the heavy traffic would go over the new line on account of the grades being better.

The hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) has experience of this transportation problem, and in view of the unfavourable results anticipated by the hon. member from Antigonish, I am sure that the opinion of the hon. member for Guysborough would be heard with pleasure by the committee.

Let us hear your
opinion first.

My opinion is that the proposed line would be in the way of an improvement. The first question to be considered by the Government in planning a road of this kind is the public interest;
the second, the interest of the district immediately served locally.

My hon.friend says
the proposed road would be in the way of an improvement. Perhaps it would, if on the new road you have six-tenths and five-tenths grades as against one per cent and upwards on the old road. But the hon. gentleman does not meet the point: can the present road be put in proper condition?
Any road can, if you spend enough money.
Has the minister any estimate of what it would cost to put the road in good condition for heavy freight?
No.

Has he ascertained
whether the present road could be put in just as good condition as the present line through Guysborough county? If he has not, why does he give the assurance now that the heavy traffic is going to go through Guysborough county?

I think I was understood by the members of the committee when I said that the grades on the proposed line will be lower than those on the present line; naturally the heavy traffic would go on the line having the lightest grades. My hon. friend knows as well as I know that you can put any grade you like on a road if you have enough money, but the operation might come to be too expensive.

Why has not the
minister obtained an estimate of what it would cost to put the present road in reasonably good condition for the carrying of heavy freight?

Demands have been
made every session for the road which we are proposing to build. We have spent a good deal of time in selecting the best possible route, because, as I have often stated, a mistake is often made in spending too little money on surveys, and a thorough survey results in the securing of better grades. The necessity for reducing the grades on the other line has not arrived. In the future it may be necessary to look into the point raised by my hon. friend with regard to cutting down the grades, but that necessity has not yet arisen; it is in the interests of the province and of the whole country that we proceed with this

new line. Later, as I have said, the question brought up by my hon. friend might be considered.

Why did the minister
select the route down the East river of Pictou instead of the West river of St. Mary's?

Simply because the
route which we have chosen runs through a productive country; on the other side it is barren.

I do not think my
hon. friend is well posted in regard to that matter. There is a stretch of forest between the two valleys.
Is there a settlement on that side ?

If the minister calls the forest barren, there may be some truth in that, but when you reach the St. Mary valley at the West river you strike very fine farming country. I am not sure it is altogether as weld cultivated as east of St. Mary; there may be an advantage in that respect, but it is not barren by any means. There is a fertile valley running down the West river of the St. Mary, capable of high cultivation. I do not think that the minister would have made .any mistake in taking the route down the West river. I was wondering if any other reason had been placed before the minister by his engineers for selecting that route.
No.

Apart from the question of route I am delighted with the announcement that the minister has made in this matter. This question has given me a great deal of concern all through my public life. For more than twenty years I have taken a very deep interest in railway communications in my native county, and I was very much pleased some four years ago to have the late Government take the matter up and decide to embark on the building of branch lines, and this one in particular. It was very gratifying to me that $1,000,000 was placed in the Estimates in 1911 to build a road into my constituency, and a decided step was taken at the time by purchasing the Sunnybrae branch at a cost of $100,000. The branch was conveyed to the Government by the Nova Scotia Steel Company; the money was paid and the deed delivered, I understand, prior to this Government coming into power. A contract was made for the con-
struction of a part of the line and a deposit of money made by the contractor. Notice was also given for the expropriation of a right of way. After my hon. friend accepted the portfolio of railways he saw fit to cancel the vote of $1,000,000, and he also saw fit to cancel the contract made with the company, and gave notice to the proprietors of the land that the expropriation of a right of way would not now go on. This delayed all progress for four years. I regret now that the right of way was interfered with, because it will now delay construction. I know that my hon. friend from Queens-Shelburne (Mr. McCurdy) wants me to say if I am satisfied with the present route. I am so much pleased to have any kind of a railroad built into my constituency that I shall heartily support the minister's proposals. I may say, however, that the proposal of the lalte Government was quite satisfactory to me and to my constituents, and it did not involve any change in the position of the main line which for many years has been the main artery between Cape Breton and Halifax. The former proposal was to build a branch line from Ferrona, in the county of Pictou, to Guysborough, which as my hon. friend knows, is a . seaport, with a branch from the cross roads of Country Harbour to the deep waters of Country Harbour. That proposal in the meantime was very satisfactory to my constituents in the county of Guysborough. They did not expect anything more than that at the time, and it was not proposed that any change should be made in the main line or the traffic on the main line. I would be glad if the minister were in a position to push forward the proposal of the late Government. That would be quite satisfactory to me. I wish to get all the railway accommodation I can for my constituency, but at the same time the member for Queens-Shelburne will understand that the old proposal was accepted by my constituents and myself and was satisfactory in every way. It did not interfere	in any way
with the rights or future prospects of the	present line	between	New
Glasgow and the strait of Canso. I notice that on the map the minister has a dotted line from Guysborough to Canso. I would like to know what his proposal is in regard to that line. I have no doubt that the minister is aware that there are great possibilities of traffic at Canso, that there is perhaps no other point in eastern Nova Scotia where the fish traffic could be de-

veloped to such an extent. If you look at the map you will see that it juts out into the Atlantic adjacent to the very best fishing ground that we have on the coast of America. You will also see that the fishing banks are directly outside of Canso and around it and that it is the most convenient place for fishing vessels to call and transship their cargoes. If we had a railway from Ferrona direct to Canso where the fresh fish could be shipped and put absolutely fresh aboard refrigerator cars bound for western points, I have no doubt it would, to a large extent, revolutionize the fish traffic in this country and give good haddock and codfish to the people not only of this province but of the West as well. The growth of the traffic has proven very satisfactory under the present accommodation. Not very many years ago there was only a boat three times a week connecting with the Intercolonial railway at Mulgrave, but under the late Administration a daily boat was put on the line and it is furnishing to a limited extent accommodation for fish traffic. On the establishment of a daily boat the fish traffic of Canso sprang to the front and it is now one of the most profitable branches of traffic from eastern Nova Scotia to the West on the present lind of the Intercolonial. It could be enormously increased by giving direct accommodation to Canso. As my hon. friend has the reputation of doing big things, might I suggest to him that instead of giving us half an apple now he give us a whole one and project the line right through to Canso?

I am sure the committee has listened with interest to the remarks of my hon. friend from Guysborough, even though they have something of a local flavour. He did not, however, correctly divine the thought in my mind. I like to see credit for public improvements go where credit is due. What I wanted to ask was the date when the purchase of the Bunny-brae road was arranged for by the late Government and when payment was made, and whether he had any knowledge of the surveys which would necessarily precede that purchase.

I think the negotiations were going on while Parliament was in session during the winter of 1911, and that the purchase was made in the following spring, but I cannot give the exact date. As to the other question, the survey was completed from Guysborough to Sunnybrae, but there was a difference of opinion whether the road should go down the eastern or the
western branch of the St. Mary's river. The late Government decided to divide the contract inter two and they advertised for tenders for constructing the eastern end of the road from Melrose, I think, to Guysborough with a branch to the deep waters of Country Harbour. The western end was not let because the question whether to go down the east or the west St. Mary's river had not been decided.
Perhaps the minister can tell when the payment was made for the Sunnybrae road?.
On the 20tli September, 1911.
The deathbed act of a dying government.

There are three sections of railways in Nova Scotia that have been somewhat travelling together for the last few years. They are the Guysborohgh road, which has been receiving some attention here to-day, the Dean Settlement and Dartmouth road, and a section of road in the county of Victoria, which is part of the riding I have the honour to represent. Ever since I have been in the House one of my principal objects has been to obtain better railway accommodation for the county of Victoria, which at present is almost absolutely void of railway facilities. We should have no railway at all if it were not that the Intercolonial railway, by sheer necessity, touches the western end of our county. It is like the old story that to get to a certain district you must needs go through Samaria, not because of any profit there is to Samaria, but simply because you have to go through there to get to some other place. Similarly the Intercolonial to get to Sydney, has to skirt the western end of Victoria county, and that is all the railway accommodation we have. The minister is well aware that in 1911 the projects in those three places were about to be materialized and the contracts let. I understand that a contract was given in Halifax, and in Guysborough, but at any rate the tenders were in, whether they had been accepted or not, when the change of Government took place. The Dean Settlement and Dartmouth railway has been proceeded with, but the Guysborough and the Victoria roads have for the time being been abandoned. I am pleased that the minister has announced to-day that at all events a second step is to be taken in carrying forward the railway policy of the former Government in the eastern part of Nova

Scotia, and that the Government is going to provide the railway facilities so long sought for and so persistently fought for by the hon. gentleman who to-day represents that county. Although there was a change of Government, I myself did not let up upon the proposition of a railway in the county I represent, and last year I moved a resolution in this House, as appears at page 540 of the Votes and Proceedings of the House. The resolution read :
That, in the opinion of this House, the time has arrived for the extension of the Intercolonial railway of Canada into the nonrailway sections of the Maritime Provinces within reasonable range of the said railway.
And the question being put on the said motion, it was agreed to.
That resolution of mine was accepted by the minister and by the Government, and I have no doubt that the vote which the minister says will be found in the Supplementary Estimates is to further implement the policy of the former Government, and to implement this resolution of mine which was accepted on the 16th March, 1914. My purpose in rising is to ask whether the minister, in providing for the extension of the road into Guysborough, has made the same provision for the extension of the railway into the county I have the honour to represent.
I am sorry to say I have not. We have not had the surveys checked up, and we have not a vote this year for such a road.

The minister last year had a party of engineers surveying from Mulgrave to New Glasgow along the present line of railway, about the same time that Guysborough county was being surveyed. They also surveyed along the South River valley from South River station, on the Intercolonial, to Cross Roads, Country Harbour, where this new line was proposed to be run. I am sure the minister must have some report from his engineers, and some sort of estimate from them as to what it would cost to reduce the grades on the present line of railway. There must also be some report in the department on the proposed branch line from Cross Roads, Country Harbour, to South River. That road has been advo- ' cated by me ever since I have been in the House. There would be no engineering difficulties in building the road, and it would run through a well-populated, magnificent agricultural section that is badly in need of railway accommodation. I do not want the minister to think that I am for a

moment suggesting opposition to the road running through Guysborough. What I am complaining about is that the minister, when his attention was called to the fact that it was necessary on account of the grades of the Intercolonial railway to find another route, did not make an effort to get the grades on the Intercolonial railway reduced. If he had done that, gone on witli his proposed road from Sunnybrae to the strait of Canso, and built a branch line from South river to Cross Roads, Country Harbour, that section of the country would have been fairly well accommodated for tile present with railways. Later on, of course, a branch would have been required to Canso, and some other branch lines.

I have sent out to see whether there is any information in the department with reference to it. If the hon. gentleman will just let his question stand for a while, I will give him later what information we have.

I would like to ask the
minister a question with reference to the surveys which were made last year between Sydney and St. Peter's. What is the situation there? There is a company road operated from Point Tupper to St. Peter's. Is it the intention of the minister to put anything in his Estimates for a road from Sydney to St. Peter's.

We had a survey made with the view of reducing the grades on the main line and also a survey made from Mulgrave down by St. Peter's canal. I am sorry that the surveys do not prove as good down by way of St. Peter's as we expected. The road would cost considerably more than we thought it would in the first place. Then it was found that to get a .06 grade on the main line it would cost $58,000 per mile. The question has not been settled and, without saying positively, the conclusion that we shall likely come to will be to put in heavier bridges. If you put on heavier rolling stock you must have heavier bridges.
On the main line?

On the main line. I
think the engineers are pretty nearly prepared to recommend that we put in heavier bridges. If we built another line we would have to keep this line open as well, and it is believed that it would be more economical to put in heavier bridges on the main line and put on heavier rolling stock.

Could the minister give me any information in regard to

the proposed line from Orangedale on the Intercolonial to Cheticamp?
An engineer went over the line this summer, but unfortunately I have not his report with me. I will be able to answer my hon. friend's question before the Estimates are through.
When does the contract with Mr. Gutelius as manager of the Intercolonial railway expire?

He was engaged first
for two or three years-I think three years- and his engagement continues as long as he and the Government work together.
Has the first three years' engagement run out?
I think it will run out in May, or in three years from the time he started. I do not remember the date he started.
Is the minister going to renew the contract?
We are perfectly satisfied with him.

I have taken the ground in this House before, and I am taking it again, that Mr. Gutelius is not giving service on the Intercolonial railway commensurate with the salary he is receiving. While the minister is satisfied with him as a railway man-and I have no doubt in the world that he is a good railway man- the people of the Maritime Provinces are not satisfied. I am in good company in this opinion because I am in the company of the hon. member for Colchester (Mr. Stanfield). I have always taken the stand before I came to this House, and I have done so since I came to this House, that there are men in the employ of the Intercolonial railway who are as well fitted to be placed in the position of general manager of the road as any importations which can be made by this or any other Government. I took that position two years ago. I believe that in the interest of the Intercolonial railway men who have grown up in its employment, bright, brainy men, who know the conditions of the road and who know the people that the road has to serve, should be given the opportunity of advancement to high positions when the time for opening these high offices comes. Men have grown up on the Intercolonial who have been obliged to leave that railway because they could not get the promotion which
they were entitled to. They have gone to other railways, to the Canadian Pacific railway and the Grand Trunk railway, and have made good there. I am not blaming the present Minister of Railways and Canals. I think the last Government sinned along the same lines, but not so grievously as has this Government. The Truro Citizen, which is the personal organ, I understand, of the hon. member for Colchester, has taken this matter up. While the Truro Citizen is spreading broadcast through the Maritime Provinces that this Government is not doing the proper thing by the Intercolonial railway, or by the Intercolonial railway men, it seems rather strange that the gentleman whose personal organ this is would not take this matter up in the House. It is all very well for him, and for his paper, to criticise the Minister of Railways in a publication which the minister perhaps never sees. I am going to read a few things that appear in this paper, and here is one of them:
Instead of removing Intercolonial Railway Company grievances rampant in 1911, the Government, if anything, has increased them, Instead of putting a stop to importing officials there has been an increase in imports. Of the old and tried officials in office in 1911, but three remain, so far as I can learn, viz., L. B. Archibald, superintendent of pullman, dining and parlor car service; D. A. Storey, district freight agent, and Owen Cameron, claims agent. All the others have been retired, including David Pottinger, and men imported to take their places; and In doing so I have no hesitation in saying that there was some rank injustice practised, injustice to men who entered the ranks as boys and spent years in trying to get to first positions. The present system has entirely killed merit on the Intercolonial railway. It does not come. The merit man finds himself supplanted by an importation.
Some may say we have not the so-called natives capable of filling important positions. Rot of the worst kind. Not long since there was published in these columns a list of young men who left the Intercolonial Railway Company, or were driven out, who went west and rapidly rose to first positions on company roads. Is there any person verdant enough to believe that these young men exhausted our supply of brainy, of capable men? It was only the other day that Grant Hall, driven from the Intercolonial Railway Company, went to a very important position in the service of the Canadian Pacific railway.
Now if brains, ability, count with western company roads, and they do, why do those roads, which always pay big salaries for the right men, let clever men go to join the Intercolonial Railway Company? If the men who have been imported for the Intercolonial Railway Company were such wonders, how came it that the company roads let them go? I am not attacking the ability of the so-called imported officials, not at all, I believe they are
Did you go?

I would really like to have the assistance of my hon. friend for Colchester in this matter. I rather think his words and his opinions would have more effect than mine would, if he were to tell the minister point-blank what he thinks about the present management of the Intercolonial.	.

There is another long article in this paper under a date subsequent to that of the article from which I have read, in which he sets forth the reasons why the Intercolonial was built. He says that the >ninister ,does tnot understand thte constitutional principles that surround the Intercolonial railway. He tells the minister that that road was built for the people, an(l that it was not intended that the Intercolonial should be made a railway for the payment of surpluses. He is a very strong party man and is in favour of the present Government along other lines; but he thinks that the Minister of Railways, being from Ontario, does not really understand the Intercolonial. I am not going to take such a local stand as that. I believe the Minister of Railways understands perfectly well the intention of the builders of the Intercolonial, and the intention of the people who had to do with Confederation in this country in regard to the Intercolonial. I am not going into the history of the Intercolonial, nor of the various discussions that took place at Confederation on behalf of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick as to the future conditions which should surround the Intercolonial. Suffice it to say that if the people of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick at that time could have foreseen Itlie developments along the lines of a corporation railway which have come and found themselves around the management of the Intercolonial in times past, I do not believe that either one of those provinces would have entered Confederation. That is an old question, and I am not going into it. The management of the Intercolonial railway at the present time may be all right, in so far as a business policy is concerned, that is, in the way of increasing freight rates and so on; but the policy of the Government, in so far as importations of men to be put over the heads of men who have grown up with the system, is not a wise policy; it will be detrimental to the best interests of the Intercolonial railway, because it will result in men coming to the conclusion that there are no avenues for promotion on that railway, and they will not take the same keen interest in their business as they have been taking in the past. The result will be that men who have grown up in the service of The Intercolonial will go to other railways. That will be a disastrous thing for the Intercolonial, because there are no men more qualified to manage its own affairs than are the men who have grown up with the sys-

tem. It is unfair to them as well as being an unwise policy. In so far as my views are concerned, I am in good company; I am with my hon. friend's, or his friends are with me in the matter. I am not finding fault with Mr. Gutelius; I am not saying that he is not a good man to manage the Intercolonial; but for a good salary the minister could get a man out of the service as well qualified and capable as is Mr. Gutelius, and those men should have the choice.
I have no doubt the Minister of Railways did not see the paper of his friend from Colchester, and I believe I could interest him by reading the very nice things it says about his department in regard to the management of the Intercolonial. Some of them are small matters, and I am not going to read them to the minister. Some of them are matters of more importance; but I have read what I think most helps my case in this regard, that is, that the policy of the Intercolonial railway and of the Government, should be to give to the local men from Nova Scotia and New Brunswick and Quebec, through which that road runs, the chance of promotion. If it is a fact, as is set out by the paper of my hon. friend, the member for Colchester, that only three chief officials of that road have been retained by this Government, it is time that the people of this country asked for a chance in the management of the Intercolonial railway.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to recall to the attention of the Minister of Railways a question I put last year at a time when he was absent from the House. It was about the difficulties which passengers from the province of Quebec, between Campbellton and Montreal, encounter in the dining cars of the Intercolonial. Complaints come daily from Frenchspeaking people who, like persons of other nationality, desire to (take dinner on board, but cannot make themselves understood by the waiters. Only last week, two ladies who arrived here were telling me that they had taken their dinner on board the Intercolonial, and although they had paid the price they had been only half served, because the waiters could not make out what they asked and the menu was drawn up in English only. This has been the case for the last fifteen years. But that the abuse lias lasted so long is no reason to perpetuate it. It seems to me that it would be easy to have on every dining car a man who understands French to help the passengers who do not understand English. In this
connection, I shall quote from a correspondence published in " Le Progress du Golfe " of the 5th of February last. The heading is:	French on the Intercolonial.
Here is an extract:
Mr. Editor:-I think I read, a few weeks ago, in the columns of your valuable paper, that the Railway Commission had at last consented to provide for French Canadian passengers on the Intercolonial a dining-car service that would meet with their just requirements.
But you can imagine my surprise and indignation in realizing last week that no change in this respect had taken place on the dining-cars of the Intercolonial. I vainly insisted on being given a menu drawn up in French ; I was told there was none. I persisted in speaking French: they stupidly answered that they did not understand.
I grant that the author of this letter is perhaps a little too exacting. It would as a matter of fact, be quite expensive to have menu cards which change every day, printed in both languages. The English menu card might do, provided there be someone around able to translate it and it would be a secondary matter, provided there were some waiter who could understand French.
Every one knows that half of the Intercolonial line is through the province of Quebec, from Montreal to Metapedia. Very often our compatriots are put to that sort of inconvenience in travelling in that section of the country. There ought to be in the dining cars at least one man-preferably the conductor-who understands French. Waiters are changed oftener and it would be better if the conductor were the one to understand French. Conductors of dining cars should be made to learn some French. It is easy enough; we ourselves learn to speak English. With a little knowledge of French, this conductor should be useful to all the people travelling on that line. He need not be a French scholar, it would be sufficient for him to be able to speak a few words of French so as to make himself understood by passengers.
As on board the trains of the Canadian Pacific railway.

But there
is here more than a question of public convenience, there is a question of revenue. If only ten persons travelling on the line from Campbellton to Montreal do not take their dinner on board, because they cannot be understood by the waiters, it is so much lost to the railway. This improvement saould have been made fifteen years ago when dining cars were put on the line. Because it has not been done, is no reason why it should not be done now.

Now, Mr. Speaker, I would call attention to the time-table of trains leaving Montreal. There may be serious reasons of which I am not aware and I should be glad to know them, I refer to the time when the maritime express leaves Montreal, which is 8.45 a.m. This train used to leave at twelve. But this was changed a few years ago and 8.45 a.m. is the present time of departure. That time is not in the interest of the Intercolonial, because it precedes by fifteen minutes the arrival of the Pacific train from the west. On that western train, which comes into Montreal at 9 a.m., there are always many passengers who are going east. What is the result? Some of these passengers continue on the Canadian Pacific railway instead of taking the Intercolonial, or if they wish to travel by the Intercolonial, they have to wait in Montreal for twenty-four hours, especially when the Ocean Limited is out of service. Even if the Ocean Limited is running, travellers from the West have to wait about twelve hours. I can see no reason why the maritime express should not leave at 10 o'clock, thus giving passengers from the west time to go from one station to the other and take the Intercolonial. I believe there would not be any great inconvenience in changing the timetable as I suggest. I did not have the opportunity of discussing the matter with the superintendant of the road. If there are serious objections I should be glad to know them. The present time-table occasions a loss of time to the travelling public and a loss of money to the treasury. Now, a word about another anomaly. The service on a section of the line which runs through my constituency is performed by New Brunswick people. Every one sticks to his own people and his own province; so I would plead for my own compatriots. The time has arrived for a change here. In olden times the Metapedia valley was an uninhabited desert, and naturally officials had to be selected from New Brunswick; but to-day things have changed and this mode of selecting officials should change also. Yet those New Brunswick employees do not speak French. Thus the superintendent and foreman do not speak French and those who work under them are all French Canadians. I cannot see why that section of the Intercolonial should not be under the control of the superintendent at Levis. If that would be giving him too much, a second division could be made comprising the line from Campbellton to Montreal under a French Canadian superintendent. 
That course could now be easily justified, because the superintendent at Campbellton has been .given a good deal more work since there has been leased by the Intercolonial one hundred and ten miles of railway going to St. Leonard, New Brunswick. It seems to me that this is a sufficient reason for giving control of the Quebec part of the Intercolonial to a Quebec man.
That is the occasion of much inconvenience to the farmers, for the passengers on the Intercolonial and to the patrons of the road who have to talk business with the superintendent, or the foreman either about fences or other works on the road and cannot make themselves understood. The same necessity was not always felt, because the land was not yet settled, but to-day the land is taken up and a change of method is urgent.
There is another defect I wish to bring to the minister's attention. That defect, or rather flaw in the Government railways legislation, has been discovered by the superintendent at Campbellton. When the farmers applied to the superintendent to have railway crossings placed at the end of their property with a proper grading, the superintendent always answered them during the last ten years that the law allowed it only for private companies and not for Government railways. So the farmers cannot have their crossings and cannot force the Government to make the necessary grading. I looked personally over the Act and I found that, as a matter of fact, it is silent in that respect as regards Government railways, while providing for private companies. It seems to me that the Government should not take advantage of this defect in the law to refuse the request of the farmers for proper crossings.
I will close my remarks, Mr. Chairman, by asking the hon. Minister of Railways to kindly grant us, as soon as the country's finances will allow and with the least possible delay, the favour of acquiring by purchase or lease the small railway from Sainte Flavie to Matane. Serious inconveniences are suffered by passengers and shippers who, because the road is operated by a company, have to pay double rates and experience long delays in the delivery of the freight. I submit it would be in the interest of ithe Intercolonial either to rent or purchase this shore line which cannot be very expensive.
It crosses a great section of my county fairly well populated and prosperous. The acquisition of this short line would work to the benefit of the Government and of the whole district.

I wish to say a few words on the subject of the general management of the Intercolonial railway which has been brought up by my hon. friend from South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll.) I do not profess to be an expert in railway matters, but this question of the general management of the Intercolonial is a very interesting one in the Maritime Provinces, especially at this time, and I believe there is no constituency more interested or more concerned in it than my own. I am not here to say anything of an unkind or harsh nature in regard to Mr. Gutelius, the manager of the Intercolonial railway. I have not the pleasure of his personal acquaintance, and therefore know nothing about his ability in his line. But from the information I have, information which I believe to be reliable, the management of the Intercononial railway for the last few years has not been of a character best calculated to promote the interests of the road. When I first had any thing to do with public matters the Intercolonial railway was operated under the management of Mr. Pottinger. I freely admit that within the last few years the Intercolonial railway has enlarged and we are having more and better trains than in the old times; but down to 1911, and even to 1912, Mr. Pottinger was at least a very prominent figure in the management of the railway. I believe that somewhere about the year 1908-the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) will correct me if I am wrong-a change was made and the management of the Intercolonial railway was entrusted to a commission, of which commission Mr. Pottinger was a member. This went on for some time, and different men were brought in from outside, and also some of our own men were chosen to be members of that board. I did not see any advantage in that form of management. Strange to say, in the election of 1911, the candidate of the Liberal party in the county of Westmorland condemned the commission form of management of the Intercolonial railway and declared that it would be better to have one man at the head of the concern as general manager. The candidate of the Conservative party in that constituency declared that the commission must go. More than that, he pledged himself that if there was a change of Government we should, have a Maritime Province man as Minister of Railways. As we all know, the Liberal candidate in Westmorland was successful but the Liberal Government was defeated. Yet, strange to say, the gentleman who at that time was particularly discussed, Mr. Brady-against whom personally I have not a word to say-instead of being dismissed as had been promised	by	the	Conservative candidate,	has	been	promoted and his
salary increased, and a house has been purchased or leased for him, and a large expenditure made to keep him living in luxury. And now, as the hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll) has said, a stranger has been brought in as general manager. The hon. gentleman refers to him as an "importation." If I refer to him in that way, it is with all due deference and not in a slighting way. I do back up
5 p.m. and corroborate, however every word that my hon. friend from South Cape Breton has said-in my opinion there are just as good men who have been in the employ of the Intercolonial railway, men who have been retired from the Intercolonial railway to make room for this gentleman, who are just as good in their line and just as capable of managing the Intercolonial railway as any man who could be brought in from anywhere outside of this Dominion. I may be wrong, but that is my strong conviction. Not only do I object to this man being brought in, but I go further and say that in my opinion the salary of Mr. Gutelius is altogether too large a sum to pay for the management of the Intercolonial railway. I am not here to talk, small politics, but I believe I am voicing the sentiments of my constituents and of the people of the Maritime Provinces generally when I say that, particularly under present conditions, the salary of Mr. Gutelius is far larger than it ought to be.

How much is he
getting?
$20,000 a year, is it not?
Yes.
Besides his salary of $20,000 a year, as my hon. friend has said he is provided with a private car, with a porter and servants-
Have not the superintendents and others always had their private cars? There is nothing new in that.

I was going on to say when the minister interrupted me-and I want to be fair; I am discussing this exactly as I feel about it-that I have no objection to the general manager having his private car; I believe it is only proper and right

that he should have it, and I should be surprised if he did not. But I do not believe that it is in the interest of the Intercolonial railway, nor do I believe that it is in accordance with democracy as we have it in this country, that the general manager or any other official, if he wishes to go from Moncton to Amherst to address a public meeting, should go in his private car and take his servants with him. Nor is it necessary, when an official of the Intercolonial is called upon to go to Prince Edward Island, to have his private car attached to the train and taken to Pointe du Chene to take the boat. And when he wishes to return, I do not think it is necessary that he should wire back to have his private car sent from Moncton to Shediac, a distance of seventeen miles, to bring his lordship back to the city of Moncton. My hon. friend smiles. But I can tell him that that.has been done. I want to be fair: it was done not only under the present Government but under the late Government, and I opposed it then just as seriously as I do now. I believe the time has come when the Government will do well, the Minister of Railways particularly, though he is not a Maritime Province man, to take enough interest in the maritime provinces to let these people understand that they are being paid by the people and that they are the servants of the people and should not impose upon them in this matter.
I go a step farther. I fear that governments and cabinet ministers sometimes forget the time when they represented constituencies and had to look after the small things of those constituencies. In the same way, I believe that one of the disadvantages in bringing in these men from outside to manage the Intercolonial railway is that they are apt to forget that they have under them men who are struggling to meet bare expenses while they are living in luxury. It is all very well for Mr. Gutelius to draw down his $1,666.66 every month in the year, and besides that he has a free house, free fuel and everything in connection with the running of his house.
That is not true.

I am subject to correction
in that respect. He gets his house free I suppose?
I think so.
And his fuel?
No.

Mr. Gutelius draws, as I
say, $1,666.66 every month. Compare this with the amount paid to the average employee of the railway, who, working ten hours a day, must work three years in order to draw as much as Mr. Gutelius draws in one month. When these workingmen come face to face with that, consideration, then they begin to doubt that they are properly treated by the Government. The feeling is growing in the Maritime Provinces and in my own county that men who are working on the Intercolonial railway are not receiving the pay that they should receive, while officials of the railway in higher positions are being paid more than they ought to receive. Under those conditions, it seems to me, the policy of bringing in outside men and putting them over the heads of men who already hold positions on the railway is one which overlooks entirely the rights and interests of Intercolonial railway employes. I bring these matters to the attention of the minister simply for the purpose of expressing the opinion that they do not constitute the proper policy for the conduct and general management of the Intercolonial railway. I believe that the Intercolonial railway was just as well conducted and managed years ago as it is now. If newspaper reports are correct, I believe that there are many more accidents than there used to be.
I want to correct my hon. friend in that. Since the " safety first " movement was introduced, accidents have been very materially reduced all round.

I am glad to have that information; I was speaking simply from my reading of reports of accidents as published in the newspapers. It does seem that the Minister of Railways would do well to take into consideration the suggestion made by the hon. member for South Cape Breton in regard to this matter. Under the circumstances I think that the minister could very well ask Mr. Gutelius to allow his salary to be reduced, particularly during these hard times, when business is dull and money scarce. I express these view's not as having the least feeling against the gentlemen who manages the Intercolonial railway. I have nothing against Mr. Brady; I know him personally and do not wish to say anything against him. But I do say that as a general thing the management of the Intercolonial railway is costing too much, and I believe that

if a change were made the people would be better satisfied in the Maritime Provinces generally, and particularly in my own constituency of Westmorland.

I do not object to any criticism made by the hon. member for South Cape Breton or by any member of the committee, no matter upon which side of the House he may be seated. I should not object to any Conservative member criticising my action in the management of the Intercolonial railway; I think the man who holds a position such as I hold to-day must expect criticism. The hon. gentleman said something about business management. I must manage the railway in a business way, because I do not know anything about managing it any other way. I have endeavoured, to the extent of my ability, to look after the interests not only of the people of the districts concerned, but of the whole people of the country. I do not suppose that anybody could manage the railway and give perfect satisfaction to everybody. I have endeavoured to keep politics out of the Intercolonial railway. I do not think it is in the interests of the line or of the people served by it that an institution like the Intercolonial railway should be run on political lines. I have held that view since I took office, and I will continue to hold to it and to carry it out. In reference to the promotion of men, one of the planks which I laid down when I first took hold of the Intercolonial railway was that promotion should take place from the ranks upon merit, and upon merit only. I am bound, as long as I am in office, to carry out that principle. I do not think that I am the only Minister of Railways who has ever been criticised, but I do not think that no Minister of Railways has gone over the system as I have gone over it and has tried to make himself as fully acquainted w.th it as I have. I have been told, though I do not know it as a fact, that other ministers-not my hon. friend (Mr. Graham) sitting over there-have had to lock the door of their car when they stopped at certain stations. I will never do that. The hon. member for Rimouski directed my attention to the advisability of having French-speaking officials on the buffet cars. I am glad he called my attention to that matter; if he had spoken of it before I should have had it adjusted, but it has never been brought to my attention. He complains about our bringing men in from New Brunswick and employing them upon the Quebec portion of the 94
railway. I do not believe that under any system you can avoid doing that, and I do not think it affects the men at all. It may be that to have on the line operating in the province of Quebec men who do not speak French would be detrimental to the service in some Tespects, but on the wohle I think it is better for the men to move round and to have this added opportunity of studying their work and becoming more efficient in it. I could not follow the hon. member for Rimouski in all his remarks, but I will refer to his speech when translated and take note of what he has said. In reference to the remarks of the hon. member for Westmorland with regard to the purchase of a house for Mr. Brady, I may say that the house was bought because of the subway to which reference has been made. The damages which were occasioned to the house necessitated its purchase, but Mr. Brady is paying rental for the house, just the same as other employees are paying rental for theirs. I think there is nothing wrong in leasing him the house, even if he is an official of the railway. My hon. friend referred to private cars. I think that when he studies the railway question a little further he will find that it pays to have a private car for the superintendent. Without exaggerating, I think Mr. Gutelius receives 300 letters a day, and when he travels in a private oar he can have his secretary and other officials with him and may attend to business all the time. I know he has done this, because I have made trips over the road with him. I am sure that any one who has had anything to do with the management of a railway knows that it pays for the manager, and even the superintendents under him, to have a car to travel in, for it enables them to perform their work much more efficiently and with greater satisfaction all round. As for the personnel, I must say that I think no railway in the land has a better class of men than is to be found on the Intercolonial. My instructions are that the men who show an interest in their work are to be watched, with a view to promotion. It is not desirable that I should bring in outside people, ,but I must say that the system introduced by the ex-Minister of Railways was not working out to advantage. With the exception of Mr. Pottinger who, like myself, was getting on in years and would in any case have had to retire very soon, we have kept on all the men who were on the old Board. Mr. Brady, who was superintendent and a member of the Board, is continued in active



work under the present General Manager. He was the man who, when I first took office, seemed to know more about the Intercolonial than anybody else. As regards the pay of the men, I do not take any credit for it, but the total amount paid in wages to-day is considerably higher than when we took office. We are getting the confidence of the men from one end of the line to the other, though of course we shall never have the confidence of them all. But the majority of them feel that we take an interest in them, that we have their welfare at heart, and are not simply trying to get all we can out of them. My hon. friend from Westmorland (Mr. Copp) has mentioned the safety first movement. I do not know anything that the men have taken a greater interest in, both for their own sake and for the sake of the travelling public, (than the safety first movement.
Notwithstanding the criticism that has been made of Mr. Gutelius, I say, and I am glad to say it, that he puts into his work all that is in him. He has satisfied me to the full. He may have made mistakes, but the man who does not make mistakes never does anything at all. He is there to work, not for any one individual, but in the interest of the whole people. I am satisfied that he gives great value for the salary he receives, and as long as I occupy my present position I propose, with the consent of my colleagues, to letain Mr. Gutelius in his position at that salary, for I think it is in the interest not only of the road, but of the whole Maritime Provinces. Where the greatest improvement has taken place is in the engineering. I do not wish to say anything about Mr. Mackenzie. He is an estimable gentleman in many ways, but I do not think he was a good engineer. If I were to criticise the construction of the Intercolonial I should say that instead of trying to get rid of grades they tried to get hold of them. It was in the engineering department that the great mistakes were made, mistakes which will cost a great deal of money to eliminate. I am satisfied that the Sydney branch could have been built very much cheaper and with much easier grades; and if that had been done our engines instead of being able to haul only 500 tons would have been able to haul 1,200 to 1,500 tons. It does not take an expert in railway matters to see how it pays to have low grades. I think that what we should study most of all is how to get the road down to a proper business basis, and how to get the most out of our rolling stock. And

as long as I occupy this position I intend to try and improve the system, to have the interests of the men at heart, and to do for the road the best that within me lies.

I have listened with a great deal of interest to the observations made by the Minister of Railways. I will supplement his statement that the unsatisfactory condition of the Intercolonial through the island of Cape Breton was due to bad engineering, by saying that the bad engineering, if such existed in the construction of the road, was due to bad politics. For it fs very well known that the location of the Intercolonial through the island of Gape Breton was purely a matter of politics. Very strong representations were made to the Government of that day that a very much better and cheaper line of railway from the Strait of Canso to Sydney could have been located through the county of Richmond and the southern portion of the county of Cape Breton. But political interests were too powerful with the Government of that day for them to accept the cheaper and more satisfactory road from every point of view, and the consequence is that the minister has to-day to deal with a railway running through the island of Cape Breton which is in the condition he has described. Last year a survey was ordered by the Department of Railways and Canals through that section of the country extending from St. Peter's to the city of Sydney, with a view to estimating the cost of a road through that section, and it was also the intention of the Government, at all events it was the intention of the late Government, to acquire the Cape Breton road, running from Point Tupper to St. Peter's, and to extend that as a Government line to Sydney. I very much regret to learn from the information which the minister has given the committee this afternoon that the report of the engineers who made that survey from St. Peter's to Sydney is unfavourable, and that owing to the cost the Government does not intend to take over the Cape Breton railway and extend it to Sydney. That will be a matter of very deep disappointment to the people living in the constituency which I represent, as well as to the people in the constituency of South Cape Breton. We have always felt that, owing to political exigencies, we were improperly deprived of having the Intercolonial pass through that section; but that injustice to that important section of the island of Cape Breton was about to be remedied by the late Government just be-

fore they went out of office. The Minister of Railways of that day had actually introduced legislation in this House for the purpose of enabling him to deal with certain branch lines in the Maritime Provinces, of which Cape Breton railway was one. Had the Government not been defeated in 1911, I am absolutely certain that the plan of the ex-Minister of Railways would have been carried out, and that to-day not only would the railway from Point Tupper to St. Peter's be operated as a portion of the Intercolonial, but I am convinced that if the extension of the line from St. Peter's to Sydney would not already have been completed it would be fairly under construction. From a statement made by the Minister of Railways this afternoon it seems there is no hope of the people in southern Cape Breton enjoying the advantages of a Government railway through that section of the country. We will endeavour to get along the best we can and hope that the day is not far distant when some relief may be afforded to the situation which exists there at the present time. While I am on my feet I should like to ask whether the minister has a report from the engineers who made the survey from Sydney to St. Peter's last summer, and if so would he be good enough to lay it on the table of the House.

I am sorry to say I
have not got it here, I shall have to get it from Moncton.

I see that the plan of the
survey of the road from Guysborough has been laid on the table of the House. I am equally interested in the report I have asked for.
All right, I will get it.

I have listened with
some interest to the observations of the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte), and while it is quite true that possibly a better line of railway could have been obtained by way of St. Peter's to Sydney, there was a great deal of difference of opinion at that time, and the final location of the road was a sort of compromise between the two sides of the island) possibly the best for the time being. I have always contended that no one railway could supply the necessities of the island of Cape Breton, as it is practically two islands divided by the sea. When there is a railway running through each arm of land, the people will have fair railway accommodation, but until that is 941	.
done the necessities of the case cannot be met. The minister refers to Mr. Mackenzie, who was chief engineer of the Intercolonial railway. I am extremely clannish to the name Mackenzie, but I must say that this Mr. Mackenzie is no relation of mine. If there were bad grades on the Intercolonial railway, Mr. Mackenzie never had anything to do with the finding of the grades. He was not in the service of the Intercolonial railway when it was built from Riviere du Loup to Halifax, or to New Glasgow. The Intercolonial railway from New Glasgow to Port Mulgrave was built by a company with which Mr. Mackenzie had no connection. The road from Port Mulgrave or the strait of Canso to Sydney was built under the supervision of another engineer; and from Montreal to Sydney, I venture to say, Mr. Mackenzie never had anything to do with the finding of the grades of the present railway. It is true he was on the road as chief engineer of maintenance and other works, but never as an engineer of construction on any part of the line. It is only fair to an old servant of the Government and the road like Mr. W. B. Mackenzie to say that he never had a chance to find any grade on the Intercolonial railway. Therefore he should not be held responsible, whatever difficulties may arise.

The minister either misunderstood my argument, or he was hardly fair in attempting to make it appear that I had argued against private cars. I distinctly said I had no objection to private cars, and would be very much surprised if they were not used by the general manager and even the superintendents of the divisions. I was complaining of the use of private cars otherwise than on business trips.
But they are doing business going and coming; the car is their office.
Would they be doing much business going from Moncton over to Pointe du Chene?
Yes, some.
Or returning from the island, would it be necessary for the superintendent or any official to wire to have a car run down to meet him at Pointe du Chene to return to Moncton? Is that reasonable?
That would take three-quarters of an hour, and he could do a lot of work in that time.

My hon. friend says he believes that to be a proper use of private cars. I take issue with him on that ground. I do not believe that is a proper use of a private car. Is it a proper use of a private car, if an official's wife wants to go from Moncton to St. John, to put a private car on an express train?
I am not going to discuss ladies here.
Does he approve of that use of a private car, and further would he approve of the use of private cars being attached to express trains to go to the golf links in the afternoons?
No, that I would not approve of, if it is true.

I am glad to have something that the minister would not approve of, and if he will inquire into these things he wrill find that what I have suggested takes place in my constituency. I wish to have it understood that I make no criticism of the general manager or other officials having private cars for use on business trips, but I do not believe that the uses which I have pointed out are proper.
Intercolonial railway-To strengthen bridges, $700,000.

When the hon. gentleman's predecessor was in office the minister was not in this House, and so he does not know what real tribulation is. His predecessor used to be abused most unmercifully in the House because he insisted on spending something on capital account, and was told on more than one occasion that the time had arrived when the capital account expenditure of the Intercolonial railway should be cut out. All these items look so familiar to me and remind me of the strong criticism that we should have no more capital account expenditures, although that criticism was not well grounded. This year my hon. friend proposes to spend on capital account between the Intercolonial railway and Prince Edward Island some $10,000,000, which is a pretty large addition to capital account. There are one or two large items, such as the works at Halifax, which come into this, but does the minister really intend to spend all of the $10,000,000 on capital account this year? There are certain items of taxation which are being imposed, because the minister says he will spend $10,000,000 on capital account. If he is going to spend it judiciously and intends to expend it I have nothing to say,

but if it is only put in lest he might want to expend it and he does not really intend to, we might reasonably not have such a great amount of taxation imposed on the country, and this item might be reduced to just enough to cover what he really intends to expend.

I think my hon. friend will agree that the expenditure at Halifax is necessary. Then there are heavy capital account expenditures at Cape Tormentine. If the hon. member had read the report on the bridges he would agree that they should be strengthened, because they have been there a long time. The bridges were not put in for the power that is being used to-day; in other words, we have been, increasing the motive power for a long time and not increasing the strength of the bridges. In many cases we have to brace up the bridges, and I think that is a very necessary item.

I am surprised that Mr. Gutelius wants to put in steel structures, because I understand that in connection with another system he thought wooden structures were pretty good. I am surprised that he should recommend steel structures for this railway. I agree that they ought to be put in. It is said that men shall answer themselves when they are in the wrong.

That will come ill at another time.
Mr. (GRAHAM: In putting in steel bridges Mr. Gutelius answers himself. Could the minister give any general idea of where the bridges are to be put in.

The following is a list of the bridges which it is proposed to put in: South iCocaigne bridge; North Coal Branch bridge; Richibucto River bridge; Kouchibouguac bridge; Barnaby river, third crossing and second crossing bridges; Bartibogue bridge; Red Pine River Bridge; Nepisiguit bridge; Tete a Gauche bridge; Beresford bridge; Elm Tree bridge; Belle-dune bridge; Dickey's bridge; Benjamin River bridge; Moffatt's bridge; Otter Brook bridge; Indian Brook bridge; Metis bridge; bridge three-quarters of a mile west of St. Anaclet; Rimouski River bridge; bridge half a mile west of Trois Pistoles; Trois Pistoles bridge.
Mr. MARCH,: Did I understand the minister to say the Restigouche river?
N'o, the Richibucto river.
Do any subways come in under this vote?
There is a different vote for those.

I understand that a slow-up order was issued to conductors on all trains of the Intercolonial railway in the month of October requiring them to slow up on all bridges and culverts between Sydney and Point Tupper, numbering 39 in all. As a consequence it is impossible for express trains to make time. It does seem rather extraordinary that all the bridges on that section of the Intercolonial railway should have gone bad at the same time. I understood that Mr. Gutelius had Been devoting some attention to the Improvement of the Intercolonial railway and it seems rather extraordinary that all the trains should have to slow up while crossing the bridges and culverts.
It was not so much that the bridges had gone bad, but the rolling stock was so much heavier than the bridges had originally been put in for.

Was there anything done
during the last year to strengthen any of these structures?

Some of them have
been strengthened this year.

Has the minister any information as to why W. Jr. Mills, of Port Hawkesbury, inspector of bridges, has been dismissed? Mr. Mills was for many years foreman-carpenter on the section of the Intercolonial railway between New Glasgow and Sydney. He was afterwards appointed trackmaster and then promoted to be inspector of bridges.

Over the whole line?
Mr. KYTE; Between New Glasgow and Sydney. I am informed that he was dismissed a week or so ago without any intimation whatever as to the reason why he was dismissed or any intimation from his over-officer that the discharge of his duties was not satisfactory. I would like to know why he was dismissed.

I will get the information.
Chatham-diversion of line and branch to wharves, $2,500.

I was very much interested in the remarks of the minister when
he said that he was looking after the interests of the people down there. I want to ask him what he has done to implement his promise made to the House one year ago. I drew his attention to the fact that he had taken up the rails on the south side of the Miramichi river and that he had left a large number of farmers and merchants without any railway transportation whatever. In his reply he stated that he had decided to operate the railway on the north side of the river only. I drew his; attention to the fact that a large river ran between the residents on the south side of the river and those on the north side and that, having taken up the rails, I said that he should provide for another approach to the line that he was operating on the north side of the river. The minister promised me ttiat he would take the matter up with the local government and see if a bridge could not be constructed across the river at Chelmsford that would provide an approach to the present line on the north side of the river.
I do not think it was I who promised that; I was not here.

Well then it must have
been the year before. It certainly was a minister, although possibly I may be wrong in saying it was the Minister of Railways. It may have been my hon. friend the Minister of Customs (Mr. Reid). At any rate a promise was made when I brought the matter to the attention of the Government. I understood that matters were so far advanced that negotiations were entered into with the local government with a view to having this bridge constructed so that there might be an approach to the railway that is running on the north side of the river. Just think of the minister taking up the rails where some 200 people reside, and who have enjoyed railway facilities for 40 years, and saying: We will not operate the road any more on this side of the river, but we will operate it on the north side of the river, and while doing this not providing any approach to the railway that he is operating! While it is true that the local government have to do with the King's highway in the ordinary sense, it is also true that the Government railway provides approaches from the King's highway to the station where it is necessary for the public to get from the King's highway to the railway.
Is it not equally fatr that he should under the present circumstances provide an approach from the opposite side of the river

to that on which the railway is now being operated ? That is a reasonable request. Generally speaking, I understood it is the duty of the local Government to provide the King's highway, but this is a matter that demands the special attention of the minister, and it ought not to be overlooked. While the minister says: I am going down there to look after the interests of the people; is he doing it in that case ? I really feel that the minister is not doing his full duty.
All right.

The Government of the day is not doing its full duty to the people living along that side of the river. Those people had railway facilities for forty years, and the Government undertook to take up the rails with the idea that it could economize and use the railway on one side of the river only; but the Government made, no provision so that the residents on the other side of the river could not reach the railway station. Moreover, there are a number of days in the fall and spring when it is absolutely impossible to get across the river under any circumstances. It is true there is a small boat ferry, and in the winter season there is the ice; but in the spring and fall there is no way of getting across. I do not know with what authority, but the rumour is going around that the roadbed that has been abandoned is to be transferred to the local authorities. When the minister replies, will he tell me if there is any. truth in that rumour ?
I never heard of application being made.

I suppose the municipal authorities or the local Government would make the application. If the roadbed were transferred, it would be done with the idea that it would be used for a King's highway along that side of the river. I want to protest in the name of the people on that side of the river against any such proposition. The people living in Chelmsford hope that some day the rails will again be laid on that roadbed. They are so grieved over this abandonment of 26 miles of railway that they hope that some day better things will come to them. We are speaking about building new branch railways. Provision is made for the Government to build new lines that do not exceed 25 miles in length without even coming to Parliament first, but letting the matter come before Parliament afterwards.
Here the Government have taken up 26 miles of rails the use of which the public have enjoyed for oO many years. I want to impress especially upon the mind of the minister that it is his imperative duty at once to arrange for an approach to the railway from the side of the river from which he took up the rails. The people who live there at the present time have no reasonable railway transportation. They have no reasonable means of getting across the river except over the ice. There is no steam ferry; there is only a boat ferry, and in order to get across the river with a team, they would have to travel about 20 miles.
Many years ago it was my privilege to support a resolution in this House in regard to transportation of fish by express. On that occasion I suggested to the minister in charge that I thought the most reasonable and feasible way would be to reduce the rates of express from the seaboard to the interior points. I am glad to say that the Government acted on that suggestion and put into force a decreased rate by paying one-third of the cost. That has been a great boon to the fishing industry and has enabled the fishermen to distribute their product in the interior of the country to some advantage. This Government should extend that policy to other towns such as Chatham and Fredericton. That, however, is not the point which I wanted to raise at this moment. I wanted to draw the attention of the minister to the fact that he can very much improve the transportation of fish. In the summer season the cars are warm and the ice melts very quickly and the fish does not arrive at its destination in as good condition as it might. Hence the whole fishing industry, as well as the transportation companies, is hurt. In the winter season, when one would suppose it would be cold, frozen fish sent by express does not arrive in as good a condition as if it went by freight. I know of customers in Toronto who, when we ask	if we shall send fish by
