express say: no; if it goes in a heated car, it will arrive in bad order; let it come by freight, although it may take ten days to reach its destination. It is in the interest of the railway as well as in the interest of the general public of Canada that an improvement should be made, because the fish will be more palatable on its arrival, and better fish will be put on the market. When the minister is having new express cars constructed he should divide them into two sections, having

MARtJH 25, 1915
a refrigerator in one section which can be simply installed with pipes and ice and salt, and it would cost very little. That refrigerator or cool room could be used in the winter to keep fish in fine condition. It could be used and kept cool in the summer, so that the ice would be preserved and the fish arrive at its destination in good order. If the minister will hear that in mind, when cars are being constructed again, it will _ help the express companies as well as the industries that are affected in the way I say. The city of Montreal and Toronto are large consuming centres, and it is important in the interest of those cities that the fish should arrive at its destination in good condition.
I want to remind the minister that there is a memorial in the office of the minister for the construction of a short line of railway from Newcastle down towards Tracadie. That section of my county is a rich one. The railway at present receives a very large benefit from the shipments of fish from Loggieville, and I am sure that if the railway were extended down on the other side of the river, it would be in the interest not only of that locality, but of the main line of the railway.
There is another matter I would like the minister to bear in mind when he is taking over the branch lines. There is a line between Moncton and Buctouche. A charter has been taken out to continue this line to Loggieville. I suppose the charter is got for the sake of what they can get out of it, for I hardly believe that any company will construct the road. But I hope the Government will some day construct that road in connection with the line between Moncton and Buctouche.
What kind of country does it go through?

Buctouche is quite a
settlement.
I mean the portions to be constructed.

A part would be wooded and the rest largely farming country. Would the minister please tell me what is to be done with the money under an item I see here for the diversion of the line between Nelson and Derby Junction?

That is to pay some
unsettled claims and also to complete a portion of the telegraph line.

The hon. minister told me that he contemplated moving Chatham
Junction to the other side of the river. Now the junction is gone, for the present at any rate. But I hope better things are in store for us in the near future. I do not wish to take up time by telling the minister that the service is most unsatisfactory. These people not only have no facilities for getting across the river to take the train, but when they get the train, the service into Chatham is very, very unsatisfactory. But I have no doubt the management are doing their very best to make it right, and I do not think it would be fair for me, at this time, to adversely criticise heir work. But there are about 10,000 people on the south of the Miramichi river, between Derby -Junction and the terminus at Loggieville, and they certainly have great lack of railway facilities. Let me give the minister an illustration. I went home a few weeks ago, I left Montreal on Saturday morning and reached Newcastle about five o'clock on Sunday morning. As the minister knows there is no train into Chatham, so I had my horse meet me.
They do not allow us to run trains on Sunday.
I left Newcastle at five, and I was home at six. If I had gone down by rail I could not have got home until seven.
Then, surely the hon. gentleman does not want more railways.
Not railways run on those lines. However, I am not finding fault at the present moment, because I know the management are doing their best.

I think the members of the various committees will expect to go on with Militia Estimates to-night, and I would ask my hon. friend (Mr. Cochrane) to look up the information I have asked for before his Estimates are taken up again. There is another matter. I have an idea that he has the same trouble with the Militia Department that I had to get them to give the business to him instead of to other roads. Could he find out how much the Intercolonial railway has received from the Militia Department for the movement of troops and so on?
I will have that for the next time my Estimates are taken up.

Thank you. I used to have my difficulties in getting the Militia Department to give us traffic.
At six o'clock, the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.
The hon. minister said that he would bring down the correspondence regarding the order for 10,000,000 rounds of ammunition, and also information respecting the censors at St. John.

I will send
over to my hon. friend the correspondence respecting the purchase of ammunition. I have the following memorandum respecting the censorship staff at St. John, N.B.:
The censorship staff at Partridge island, St. John, N.B., consists of: Charles Masters, St. John, censor ; George Shaw, St. John, assistant censor; J. Herbert Crockett, St. John, assistant censor. The censor is paid $9 per diem and the assistant censors $7 per diem.
Partridge island is a wireless station, employed only for communication with shipping. At the opening of the war it was closed, but on January 4, 1915, the chief of staff of the Naval Service Department wrote to the military Secretary of the Interdepartmental Committee, stating that it was being reopened to traffic, and asking that a censorship staff be appointed.
Delay was caused by the gentleman first offered the post of censor accepting and then declining. Mr. Masters accepted the post on January 12, 1915. Up to March 25 there is due to him $657 and to his assistants, $1,022 [DOT] total, $1,679.
Mr. Masters reports that he and his assistants are regularly at work in relays of eight hours as far as possible, the communication between the station and the mainland occasionally being irregular. There is always one member of the staff present at the station.
The number of messages handled to March 13 was 537. The volume of traffic is not great but the fact that the station is open for the transmission of wireless messages renders vigilance necessary, and it is essential to have the censor or an assistant censor present all the time to ^ ensure the absence of improper communications. The regulations for censorship state:	" the minimum number sufficient to
carry on the work of censorship at any station which is open day and night will be three." The station thus has the smallest number of censorship staff compatible with observance of the regulations.
(Sgd.) C. P. Hamilton,
Lt.-Colonel, Deputy Chief Censor.

Last evening the hon.
member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte) brought up for the second time this session the question of the alleged ill-treatment of the 17th Battalion, comprised largely of Nova Scotians, -while at Valcartier camp and Salisbury Plains. He was careful to assert that he did not bring the matter up for the purpose of casting any reflection upon the Minister of Militia. His alleged purpose-I quote from his remarks as they appear on page 1494 of Hansard-was:

I think, however, that it is only just to the persons in Nova Scotia who are interested in the 17th Battalion, made up, as it is, of Nova Scotians, that these matters should be brought to the attention of the committee and of the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence.
I cannot possibly understand how the hon. member for Richmond could feel that he was serving any purpose likely to benefit the people of Nova Scotia by bringing such a matter to the attention of the committee at this time. It must be borne in mind, without respect to the merits of the allegations that were made by him and by the hon. member for Guysborough, that no satisfactory inquiry could be made in respect of this matter until after the return of the men from the front. I think it should be borne in mind also that while this great war is in progress the discussion of matters of moment to perhaps a few men, but of comparative insignificance as affecting the welfare of the Empire, might very well remain in abeyance. However, since the hon. member for Richmond and the hon. member for Guysborough sought to make an ex parte statement, as it were, of the alleged ill-treatment of the Nova Scotians at Valcartier and Salisbury Plain, I think it only fair that a statement in reply should be submitted. For that purpose I have had placed in my hands some affidavits made by men whose names are alleged to have been signed to the memorandum submitted by the hon. member for Guysborough, and bearing particularly on the question of the alleged ill-treatment referred to. I may add that I have had nothing to do with the preparation of these declarations. If I had been preparing them myself, I should not have included some of the statements which are contained in them, but I cannot read portions of them; I must read them in their entirety. The first one is from Robert Aldridge, and is as follows:
I,	Robert Aldridge, of Toronto, in the province of Ontario, fitter, declare as follows:
1. I know Spas Stackoff and knew him since Christmas. I was suffering from asthma in the hospital and Stackoff was in the same ward with me for a month. Stackoff has told me regarding signing the document regarding the Nova Scotia Battalion. He said he did not know what he had signed and said he thought it might be regarding the helping of the sick.
I told him it was not that but I had learned it was something done for the purpose of harming the Government. I have never voted in Canada and had no political sympathy in Canada, but as I considered all the men had been treated most fairly by the Canadian and Imperial Governments, I felt that it was doing a grave injustice to circulate such a false complaint. I saw the cigar box-

The significance of that statement will appear as I read subsequent affidavits.
-but would not sign the statement which evidently had been prepared without any reference to what the men would testify if they were asked. I never heard any complaints regarding the Nova Scotia Regiment and I was ir. the same surroundings as Staekoff; and I make this solemn declaration conscientiously believing it to be true and that it is of the same force and effect as if made under oath and by virtue of " the Canada Evidence Act." (Sgd.) R. Aldridge.
Declared before me this 18th day of March, A.D., 1915.
(Sgd.) R. H. Murray,
A Commissioner for taking affidavits to be used in the Courts of Nova Scotia.
Here is the affidavit of Staekoff himself:
I, Spas Staekoff, formerly of the 9th Battalion, 1st contingent, declare as follows:
1.	I enlisted in Edmonton in the 9th Battalion and went to England to Salisbury Plain. In November I was suffering from rheumatism and went to the hospital. I never saw the 17th Battalion from Nova Scotia. I never came in contact with them and never heard anything about them in any way.
2.	The day before yesterday, Tuesday the 16th inst., I was at the barracks on Sackville street, and I saw a man with a paper and a box of cigars. I asked him for a cigar and he said "if you will put your name down on the paper I will give you a cigar." I asked him what the paper was, but he would not tell me. I thought it might be to help the sick men and I signed it and he gave me the cigar. I cannot read English but can speak it fairly well. I am a Bulgarian. I have been invalided home but I have nothing whatsoever to complain about In my treatment in camp or in hospital. I never heard any men complain of conditions, as I believe we all had to help out and the authorities were doing the best they could for us. I make this declaration voluntarily and to free my conscience of making what I learned afterwards to be a complaint concerning ill-treatment of the soldiers,- a thing which I had no idea of doing and which was absolutely false in regard to the neglect and ill-treatment. No oath or declaration was taken from me on making the declaration referred to on the 16 th instant.
And I make this declaration conscientiously believing it to be true and that it is of the same force and effect as if made under oath and by virtue of the Canada Evidence Act, the said declaration having first been read over and explained to me, and I understanding the same, in the presence of myself, Cprl. R. Aldridge and the commissioner herein.
(Sgd.) Spas Staekoff.
Declared before me this 18th day of March, A.D., 1915.
(Sgd.) R H. Murray,
A Commissioner for taking affidavits to be used in the province of Nova Scotia.
Witness,
(Sgd.) R. Aldridge.
The next is the affidavit of Wm. Thomas Oldridge, which reads:
I, William Thomas Oldridge, at present in the city of Halifax, do solemnly declare and say as follows:
1.	That my home address is London, Ontario.
2.	I enlisted in the first contingent at London, Ontario, for overseas service.
3.	I joined with the 7th Fusiliers and was transferred into the 10th Battalion and went across to England with the first contingent.
4.	I was at Salisbury Plain continually from the time we sailed from Canada until after Christmas.
5.	I have been invalided home because of illness.
6.	The lines of the 17th Battalion, Nova Scotia, and the 10th Battalion joined one another, and the men of the two battalions mingled together and were intimately acquainted. This was at Bulford Sling Plantation and Pond Farm.
7.	I heard read in Halifax yesterday to several of the men who were in the first contingent and who were invalided home with me, typewritten or printed statements which I understood had come from the office of the Morning Chronicle of this city. These statements were read to the men at the South Barracks. There would be about twenty or so men in the room. Of these only three or four were members of the Nova Scotia 17th Regiment, and these had only been transferred to the 17th Battalion two or three weeks before they had come to Halifax.
8.	The persons who had the statements, however, solicited every man in the room to sign these statements notwithstanding that the great majority of them were not members of the 17th and knew nothing of the statements. On this occasion two or three men signed.
9.	The men who had these papers for signature were supplied with a large quantity ox cigars which they were distributing freely among the returning soldiers whom they were soliciting to sign the papers.
These circumstances just now related happened on Tuesday, the 16th. While they were passing the cigars around and getting the signatures the men handling the business announced that they had further supplies down at the office, which we understood to mean the Chronicle office.
10.	These men did not receive their pay until this morning, Thursday, the 18th inst., and yesterday afternoon, Wednesday, the 17th inst., a large number of them appeared to be supplied with money and were in an intoxicated condition. I did not see any of the men receive the money but from the circumstances and conditions and statements of the men I am satisfied that some person, on Tuesday and Wednesday were supplying these men with money and liquor. They had no part of their pay at that time.
11.	Most of the statements contained in these written papers which the men were asked to sign were not true. There were some inconveniences that all the battalions had to put up with and which we all expected to put up with, but the 17th Battalion had no more of them than any other. In fact they had more conveniences than we of the 10th Battalion.
12.	During the months that we were there together mixing one battalion with the other we never heard of any complaints from, the men of the 17th Battalion that they were being badly or unfairly treated or abused.

In the absence of the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) I should like to ask my hon. friend from Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes) whether he gave my hon. friend any intimation that he was going to bring this matter up?
I did not because I did not see him. These papers have been in my possession only about two hours.

I think it is to be regretted that my hon. friend from Cumberland, before bringing to the attention ol the House this matter which I thought was thoroughly threshed out last night, did not intimate to the hon. member for Guysborough that he intended to do so. I see by Hansard that the hon. member for Guysborough read last night a paper purporting to be signed by a number of men to the following effect:
We, the undersigned officers, non-commissioned officers and men of the 17th Nova Scotia Battalion, having read the article published in the Morning Chronicle of February 25, 1915, signed by H. C. Crowell, do hereby certify it to be a true statement of the facts concerning the treatment of the said battalion, so far as our knowledge goes, and we have a personal knowledge of most of the facts therein stated:
I never knew that that statement had been made until the hon. member for Guysborough read it last night, but as my hon. friend has again brought this matter up I think that, in the absence of the hon. member for Guysborough it must necessarily involve some statement from him in regard to it. At this juncture I merely wish to point out that the basis of all this discussion in the Morning Chronicle and in this House on these two occasions was the statement made by Col. Struan G. Robertson in the first instance, and that anything that may have been attributed to these non-commissioned officers and men in Halifax as to what they did or did not say is not half so strong as what was said by Col. Struan Robertson not only in letters to his friends, but in the information lie gave to the correspondent of the Halifax Chronicle who happened to be on the other side. So that the gentleman with whom the issue rests, so far as any difficulty of good Itaste is concerned, either in this House or out

of it is Col. Struan G. Robertson. I do not propose to discuss the matter any further except to express regret that the incident has again come up in the House and to point out to the hon. member for Cumberland. who I am sure will appreciate it, that in justice to the hon. member for Guys-borough who happens to be absent, we must naturally expect to hear from him again.

speechtext:
I should like to say that the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte) introduced the subject by reading a letter addressed to myself, and neither the Minister of Militia, who is concerned in the statement, nor I had the slightest notice that he proposed to take that course, so I would not think the hon. gentlemen has anything to complain about. It is only by the merest accident that I happened to be in the House at the time when these statements were read. I have alluded to certain letters of which I had some recollection and I think it is only just that 1 should give them to the House, and I will give them in the order of their dates:
Dear Sir Robert:
The Minister of Militia showed me in London recently a letter purporting to be from myself and Major Struan Robertson. The letter was written as a protest on the part of Nova Scotia and contained strictures against the character and qualifications of the Minister of Militia. At the time that the Nova Scotians were striving to gain the authorization to form themselves into a regiment, a misunderstanding arose between ourselves and the minister as to the number of men we claimed to have brought into camp at Valcartier. Major Robertson asked me if I would sign a paper addressed to the Premier aiming to offset any mistaken representation that might have been made by the minister, and at the same time to present clearly the arguments as to why we should have a regiment from Nova Scotia. I was informed that all the other officers and non-commissioned officers were signing, and I readily affixed my name without reading, taking it for granted that the letter was as represented.
When Major General Hughes showed me a copy I was astounded as I had never sanctioned in any way such complaints and such strictures as were made against the Minister of Militia. The letter was not signed by other officers and I wish to place myself on record in repudiar tion of this letter, and I absolutely deny any responsibility for the accusations contained therein.
I am, very truly yours,
(Sgd.) C. A. Andrews. Wtst Down South Camp,
Salisbury, November 4, 1914.
That is Major Andrews?	.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Colonel Andrews,
I think. This is the next letter:

Pond Farm Camp,
Salisbury Plain, Nov. 9, 1914.
Dear Sir R-bert:
1 have just learned from Lieut.-Colonel Andrews that a copy of a statement signed by us has been received by you. It was- drawn up previous to your visit to Valcartier when we were all smarting under the unmerited treatment we had rece.ved. Tour visit rendered the completion of the paper unnecessary and I put the original and two copies aside to destroy them. I find that I have now only the original and one copy left and am utterly at a loss to know how or by whom the other copy was forwarded to ycu. I regret exceedingly that you should have been caused the annoyance of receiving the statement after all occasion for it had passed.
With regard to the rifle I brought this matter to the attention of the Adjutant General Colonel Williams who advised me to make a report in writing to Colonel Helmer. This I did. Colonel Helmer went into the matter carefully with me and assured me that the defects had been remedied by calling in the rifles while at Valcartier and adjusting the springs, while the sights were being improved so that they could no longer come apart in handling. My duty in the matter was thus discharged.
I have the honour to be, sir,
Tour obedient servant,
(Sgd.) Struan G. Robertson.
I am not absolutely sure whether this letter refers to the communication to me which has been read in the House. On reference to my files I do not seem to have any record of my having received that communication; at least my secretary informs me that he cannot find any trace of it although in replying to Colonel Robertson I seem to take it for granted that I had received it.
He seemed to take it for granted too.

speechtext:
Ottawa, Ont. November 20, 1914. Dear Colonel Andrews:
I have your letter of the 4th instant and note the information therein contained.
We are glad to know that the Canadian expeditionary force made so fine an appearance and gave so favourable an impression when they were reviewed by His Majesty the King.
I understand that Lord Kitchener spoke most warmly in commendation.
Tours faithfully,
(Sgd.) R. L. Borden.
Colonel C. A. Andrews,
West Down South Camp,
Salisbury Plain, England.
Ottawa, Ont., November 26, 1914.
My dear Colonel Robertson:
Your letter of the 9th instant reached me in due course. No copy of your communication was furnished by me to General Hughes, but from some source a copy has evidently reached

him as he has alluded to it in correspondence and in conversation.
Believe me, yours faithfully,
(Sgd.) R. L. Borden. Lt.-Col. G. Struan Robertson,
Pond Farm Camp,
Salisbury Plain, England.
Then there is a letter from Surgeon-General Guy Carleton Jones:
Office of Director of Medical Services, '
34 Victoria street, London, S.W.,
February 27, 1915.
The Hon. Sir George Perley,
High Commissioner for Canada,
17 Victoria street, S.W.
My dear Sir George:
Mr. Crowell, representing the Halifax Chronicle, came to see me on or about the 10th instant to ask some questions concerning the sanitary conditions of the camp, and more particularly as regards the 17th Battalion.
I gave him a few facts, and he then stated that he regretted that he had not come to me before, and that he thought it would be advisable for him to cable to his paper not to publish an article which he stated he had written and forwarded.
With reference to the 17th Battalion, this unit was under exactly the same conditions as all the other units of the 4th Brigade, namely, the 9th, 10th, 11th and 12th Battalions, the 3rd Field Ambulance, the Reserve Park and some other details. They were not crowded like cattle, and they were never left without a qualified medical officer.
They have had six cases of cerebro-spinal meningitis, but beyond that their health has been very good.
Yours very truly,
(Sgd.) G. C. Jones, Surg. General, Director of Medical Services,
Canadian Contingents.
Next there is a letter from Lord Kitchener's secretary, which reads as follows:
War Office, White Hall, S.W., 1-3-15. Dear Sir George:
I showed the enclosed telegram to Lord Kitchener who desired me to say that, as you surmised, the allegations of the writer in the Halifax Chronicle were quite untrue. The Secretary of State did not know whether there were any means of bringing the originator of these malicious falsehoods within the reach of the law for, of course, such statements were calculated, if not strenuously denied, to have bad effects.
Yours sincerely,
(Sgd.) H. J. Creedy.
The telegram alluded to in this letter is that which I have already read in the House. It was a telegram despatched by me to Sir George Perley, setting forth in substantial detail the allegations contained in the newspaper article alluded to. There is also a letter from General Alderson a portion of which has already been given to the House, and which is as follows:
France, March 7, 1915.
Dear Sir George:
I have your letter in which you send a copy of a cable from the Prime Minister regarding the 17th Battalion.
Were it not serious in that it gives the people of Nova Scotia a totally wrong impression, the article in the Halifax Chronicle would be as childish as was the idea, that you told me of, that trenches round tents were not allowed on Salisbury Plain, because they would interfere with the hunting.
The only word of truth in the whole article is that Colonel Robertson has been replaced.
The fact that these units knew that they were not coming with the division naturally dampened every one's spirits, and I have no doubt some of the men, in writing home, would overdraw the picture of the inevitable difficulties and discomforts.
All the nonsense about being used as scavengers, etc, is pure invention.
Tours sincerely,
- (Sgd.) E. A. H. Alderson.

Just one word which I feel it due to myself to say in response to the statement of the hon. member for Piotou (Mr. Macdonald). I think I realize quite fully that courtesy and consideration which ought to be extended by one member to another in this House on whichever side he may be, and therefore I would be the last person in the world who would wish to offer discourtesy to the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) or to any other hon. member. But I did not feel that this was a matter affecting the hon. member for Guysborough. It is a matter of public interest that affects everybody, that affects the people of Nova Scotia in particular, and I did not feel that it was incumbent upon me to advise the hon. member for Guysborough that I proposed to read these affidavits in the House any more than it was incumbent upon him to notify me that he proposed to make a statement last night. He did not notify me, he did not notify the Prime Minister, and he did not notify the Government or any member of it.

My hon. friend (Mr. Rhodes), I know, is very courteous, and I have always recognized that. Unfortunately, at the time my hon. friend spoke, my hon. friend from Guysborough was not here, and I thought that the tone of his utterances and the reading of the affidavit would be to a certain extent matters of interest to my hon. friend because these affidavits related to a statement which he had read in the House last night.
Not to the statement of the hon. member for Gyysborough.

No, but the statement which he had read to the House. This is not a question reflecting upon the people of Nova Scotia. Colonel Struan Robertson undertook to make certain charges to the Prime Minister, and he wrote to his political friends in the House acquainting them with these charges. He communicated these facts to a correspondent of a newspaper in the city of Halifax with the desire of having them made public. That is why they were made public. That is why we had the discussion here, and it is just as well to understand that if there have been any complaints it is no use blaming newspapers or anybody else. Colonel Robertson was the gentleman who inaugurated these complaints and who has persisted in reiterating them.

I regret very much that I did not hear the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes) when he spoke, but I understood that he produced some statements from parties who had signed the memorandum which I read to the House last night, qualifying in some way the memorandum which they had signed. I do not know these gentlemen. I am not acquainted with any of the gentlemen in question except Colonel Struan Robertson himself. He is the only man amongst these officers that I have ever met or known anything about. I do not want my hon. friend to think that I am in any way personally concerned or interested in the result of this inquiry. I was simply interested on account of the province of Nova Scotia which he and I have the honour to represent, and I feel especially interested in regard to the parents and friends of many of these young men who have volunteered for service at the front. A few days ago I visited Nova Scotia and I was surrounded by some of these people. They were interested in the young men who had gone with the 17th battalion and they were very naturally anxious as to the treatment of the boys on the other side in view of the statements that had appeared in the public press. I thought it my duty to say a few words last night to ascertain whether or not the treatment that was supposed to have been meted out by the Minister of Militia himself to these officers and men at Valcartier was such as it had been represented to be. I do not pretend to discuss what has taken place on the other side of the Atlantic. The Prime Minister in his reply deprecated the fact that I should have thought of stirring up distrust between the 
people of Canada and the officers in command of the forces on the other side. I did nothing of the kind. My right hon. friend had no right to make any such statement. Any hon. gentleman who will read my remarks will see that I was very careful not to deal with anything that happened ^ at Salisbury. I directed my remarks altogether to Valcartier and to the statements in regard to the minister himself. These statements I do not need to reiterate to my hon. friend from Cumberland because they are on record and I would like to know if he is satisfied. Is he absolutely satisfied that the Nova Scotia battalion got that fair-play and consideration that they ought to have received at Valcartier?

I wish to say that in my opinion if the treatment accorded to the Nova Scotia men was as bad as it is alleged to be, or if it were a hundred times worse, it would still be most unfortunate that the matter should be ventilated in this House at this time when we have not the men here and when a proper inquiry cannot be had. While that statement involves the officer commanding, General Alderson, and others, I deprecate the circumstance that the matter should even be mentioned in this House, and I sincerely hope that the whole thing may remain in abeyance till such time as an investigation can be had after the war is over.
My hon. friend has his minister here, and he is supporting him.
The minister has absolutely nothing to do with the soldiers once they cross the water.

The minister himself
has not said so. The minister was discussing the matter in regard to the officers of the 17th Battalion. I referred to nothing else. In my remarks I was careful not to refer to General Alderson or to any one else on the other side of the Atlantic. I wanted to elicit from the minister whether he had really treated the officers of the 17th Battalion in an unfair manner at Valcartier. My hon. friend the member for Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes) ought to be as much interested in this question as I am. He ought to feel it his duty to stand up for the Nova Scotia Battalion in this House or anywhere else. I do not wish my hon. friend to insinuate that I was the first man to commence this discussion in this House. My right hon. friend the Prime Minister spoke 6f it on several occasions before I ventured

to say anything. It was not a hew question in this House last night. It had been discussed in the newspapers throughout the country. It had been discussed by hon. members previous to last night. The remarks made by myself and by my hon. friend the member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte) last night were only for the purpose of completing the discussion commenced in this House on a former occasion.
My hon. friend was not here when I made my remarks. When he reads them to-morrow morning, he will not take exception to a single word I said.
I am glad to hear that.
I made no reflection upon the hon. member whatever.

Enough has been said
to warrant a thorough investigation to set the matter at rest and to show, the people of Nova Scotia and the relatives and friends of the men who volunteered that the latter were well treated at Valcartier. I do not wish to criticise the minister unduly, but it is due to him to institute a thorough investigation into this matter, and to lay before the House and the country the real facts, so that the relatives and friends of the young men who volunteered may feel that when they did so at the risk of their lives and of their future, they were properly treated by the military authorities of Canada.	*
Mr. MoCURDY:	I was not in the
House last evening when this discussion was first precipitated. On perusing Hansard, I find that last night a copy of a letter written to me by Col. S. G. Robertson was produced and read. I am at a loss to understand how that letter came into the hands of the party who read it. Possibly the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) can enlighten me on that subject.

Which letter?
Mr. McCURD l :	The letter addressed to
me which was read in the House last night.

I did not read any
letter in the House last night. I read only a memorial from certain privates and officers corroborating the statement published in the Morning Chronicle. I know nothing about the letter except what I heard read in the House.

It was read by the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte).
Mr. McCURDi : I am sorry that the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte) is not here. He might be able to inform us as to how he procured the letter. The discussion seems to have been left by him at an early date and to have been taken up by my hon. friend the member xor Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair). I am very sorry that this subject has become at the present moment one of public notoriety, and that my name has been introduced into the discussion through the reading of that letter, for I have up to the present refrained from participating publicly and would hate continued to do so if my name had not been mentioned in this House. The present is to my mind a time for deeds, not words.
I will state first that the letter which was read last night is a copy of one which 1 received; but some six days prior to the receipt of that letter by me, the whole matter was precipitated for public discussion by publication in the press. The whole incident is, in my opinion, unfortunate, and in this view I think I am in line with the best public opinion in the province of Nova Scotia, as well as elset-where.
It has been personally stated to me that the direct result has been an adverse effect upon recruiting in Nova Scotia. I was told by an officer of the 40th battalion that the day before the public discussion began some 37 recruits offered for enlistment, and that on the following 'day the number fell to 12. Recruiting slumped to a marked extent.
Whether or not the matter should be publicly discussed is a question upon which members may differ. I have expressed my own opinion. Whatever the reasons for publication may be. the effect is quite apparent. But I cannot see how public interest is to be served by bringing the matter up in the House at the present time.
When the articles were first made public, they were brought to the attention of the Prime Minister in the House, and assurance was given by him that he had requested that an investigation be made by the proper military authorities of Great Britain. Therefore it is difficult to understand what useful purpose could be served by having the matter brought up in the House before the finding of that court is available.
The hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) last night read a number of affidavits. He also stated that he was

east and that he came back yesterday. I should judge that the affidavits read by him were not voluntary on the part of the deponents nor, indeed, obtained without some expenditure of time and energy.
And cigars.

On a recent visit to England I had the proud pleasure of spending a few days on Salisbury Plain. If any statements have been made that the Canadians there were dissatisfied or unhappy, I can say that those statements are not correct. They have been perfectly well treated there. They had hard times owing to the inclement weather, but no more at Salisbury Plain than elsewhere. So far as the Canadian boys in Salisbury camp are concerned, they were all happy and contented and all anxious to get to the front.

I am glad to hear the testimony of my hon. friend from Quebec (Mr. Power) in regard to Salisbury. But

we were discussing the question of Val-cartier. My hon. friend from Queens and Shelburne (Mr. McCurdy) is the particular friend of Colonel Robertson- He is the man to whom the Colonel appealed. I would like to ask the hon. gentleman if he did anything in answer to Colonel Robertson's communication telling of his difficulty, and asking the hon. gentleman to assist him in his trouble. He is the man whom Colonel Robertson most depended upon to right his wrongs. I should like to know if the hon. member took any action, or did he put Colonel Robertson's letter in his pocket and do nothing? That was what was worrying me when the hon. member was giving advice to us on this side of the House to say nothing about it.

I have already told the hon. gentleman that with the idea of geographical location of units I am thoroughly in accord. I supported the proposal to organize a Nova Scotia battalion, and I have found no reason to change my mind. With regard to what he calls my particular friendship with Colonel Struan Robertson, I regret to say that I had not the pleasure of meeting the gentleman until after the first of August of last year. Anything that I have heard of Colonel Robertson's military qualifications is favourable, but it is a matter of hearsay. It was not for the purpose of advancing any one's personal interest, whether officer or anybody else, that I took an interest in the organization of the Nova Scotia regiments, but because I believed that the idea of grouping soldiers of one province in a battalion by themselves was sound and would result in more efficient service.

I desire to ask the Minister of Militia a question. Is it not a fact that all the officers and all the contingents are under the author-9 p.m. ity of the British War Office and that the Canadian authorities have nothing to do with them?
Yes.

I quite understood that my hon. friend from Queens and Shelburne was in favour of the Nova Scotia battalion, and I understood he took an active interest in the formation of the battalion at the time it was first proposed. The reason why I thought he must be in the confidence of Colonel Robertson was, that while there are eighteen members in this House from Nova Scotia, the hon. gentleman was the man selected py Colonel 95
Robertson as the one to whom to address a letter of complaint. I inferred from this that Colonel Robertson had more coofi-dence in the hon. gentleman than in any of the rest of us. I would like to know if he is perfectly satisfied with the treatment accorded to Colonel Robertson and his associates in connection with this matter.

Long before 1 received the letter to which the hon. gentleman refers, the whole matter had been placed before the public by the press and the Prime Minister immediately gave his statement to the House that he had asked the War Office for an investigation. That seemed to me to be a perfectly reasonable and logical course of action, and I have not heard that Col. Robertson is not satis-ed with this course. I am surprised that the hon. gentleman is not himself satisfied with the assurances given and the procedure taken.

It is difficult for the War Office to investigate what took place on this side of the Atlantic, and that is the matter I am asking about. Is the hon. gentleman satisfied with the treatment of these soldiers before they went across to England? That is a question that can be answered by yes or no.
In his treatment of the case last night, I understood the hon. gentleman referred both to Salisbury and Val-cartier, but possibly the reference to Salisbury was by the hon. member for Richmond.
May I ask the hon. member for Guysborough if it is not true that he himself is very much more closely related to Colonel Struan Robertson than-
I am not related to him at all.
I think that by marriage they are very closely connected. The hon. gentleman is a brother-in-law of Colonel Robertson, unless I am greatly mistaken.
My hon. friend is mistaken.
I want to say, on behalf of the hon. member for Guysborough, that Colonel Robertson is not his brother-in-law.
I did not suppose that any one thought so.

It is rather amusing to see hon. gentlemen on the other side



trying to unload Colonel Struan Robertson on the hon. member for Guysborough.

Last evening in discussing the appointment of censors, I referred t,0 the chief censor, Lt.-Colonel Hamilton, and stated that it was rumoured that he had been engaged since his appointment in writing party pamphlets. I desire to say in justice to him that I received a letter from him in which he calls attention to the report of my remarks and assures me that the rumour is entirely without foundation. I very cheerfully accept his statement and have no doubt that injustice was done to him by my giving currency to the rumour.
Militia and Defence-customs dues, $125,000.

It appears from evidence given in the Public Acounts Committee that in most cases duty has been charged on goods brought into Canada to be sent across to England and France. It is a most remarkable thing that the Government should borrow money from England for the purpose of prosecuting this war and then take a portion of that money to themselves in the way of customs duties upon goods imported into Canada to be sent across to England and France to help prosecute the war. Evidence was given that duty was paid in connection with motor transports of different kinds, amounting in the aggregate to many thousands of dollars. Would the minister explain whether there has been any fixed policy in that regard and, if so, the reason for that policy?

In the early
stages of the war our attention was not directed to these little points, although arrangements were made with the Customs Department-the Minister of Customs was only too willing to accede to the suggestion- whereby goods coming through in bulk or bond should be entered duty free. The case of trucks partly made in Canada, upon which the duty is paid by the manufacturer, is a rather complicated matter; we are looking into it. I found the other day that duty is being charged upon field glasses; it is of duty in this respect refunded by the Customs Department. We are proceeding to have this matter looked into, and whatever duty has been paid on imported articles to be used for war purposes, it is our intention to have refunded.
Refunded to the war appropriation?
Yes.
About how much money has been paid in duty on such articles as have been mentioned?	*

Not very much,
I think. It was in connection with the importation of field glasses that my attention was directed to this matter. We furnished the officers with field glasses, and I found that they were being put in at abnormal prices. Upon inquiry I found that these prices were partly due to the duty which was being paid and partly due to a combine which prevented the sale of field glasses at reduced rates. With this combine Canada has nothing whatever to do. We tried half-a-dozen times to break it; we did break it once, but I am sorry to say that we cannot break it again. Duties which have been paid upon these field glasses will be refunded.
Dominion arsenal, $300,000 .

Where is the Dominion arsenal situated, what work is being done there, and how many men are employed?
Major-General HUGHES: Salaries amount to $34,000; wages of operatives, $581,000; material, $564,000; machinery, $5,000; electricity and gas, $18,000. It is required to keep the arsenal going night and day. About six hundred men are employed.
What does the arsenal turn out?
The arsenal turns out mark vii rifle ammunition and a limited number of shrapnel shells.
Where is it?

Mr. PUGSLEY; Of course this must be borne in mind, that in the United States in times of peace, with a standing army of less than 80,000 men, their requirements of ammunition would be trifling compared with those required by the British Government as the result of the activities of Mr. J. Wesley Allison. I am told that as a result of his negotiations 200,000,000 rounds were ordered.

Government. member looks back he will see the figures are borne out relatively the same for years. What they pay to the factories is much higher than what they put down as the cost to themselves. If my hon.
friend could induce some member of the United States Congress to take that matter up I presume he would have a good field to operate in; but as it does not concern ourselves in the slightest I do not know whether we need burden ourselves with it. Our net cost paid to outsiders is higher than the figures he has given and our factory price is lower than the price in the United States, which I think shows that we have made a good bargain.

It concerns us if we find that we are paying very considerably higher

prices in Canada than the same ammunition costs in the United States, where the cost of labour and of materials would he at least as high as in Canada. It also concerns us in another way, that the British Government, which would be interested in getting ammunition at the lowest possible cost, has entrusted this Government with the purchase of ammunition for it. It concerns us if Mr. J. Wesley Allison, acting for this Government through the Minister of Militia, has committed the British Government to the payment, as my information is, *or something like $8 per thousand more than might have been arranged for if proper judgment had been exercised and proper arrangements had been made in the interests of the British Government.

The hon. gentleman

I do not know that that is any of the hon. member's business, but I will answer it. There is nothing to conceal. Mr. Allison declined to accept anything either directly or indirectly for anything he might do in connection with the Dominion of Canada. I understand that Mr. Allison has been instrumental in making large contracts with the Russian Government in the Dominion of Canada and in the United States, amounting to upwards of $80,000,000 in one or two cases. My hon. friend asks me on what I base my statement that there was a difference of eight dollars in the price at which this ammunition could have been bought for the British Government and the price at which it was actually bought. What I base my statement on was
this, and I was very careful to state when I addressed the committee last evening, and when I made a previous statement in this House, that I had no personal knowledge of the matter. I brought the matter to the attention of the Government, and, last evening, to the attention of the Minister of Militia, in order that the matter might be looked into. I am not making any charges at all, but my hon. friend will recognize that the people are entitled to get the facts in regard to purchases of war material. The statement which I made was this: that I was informed that the British Government, through a gentleman whom they had perhaps not definitely employed-perhaps it would be better to say tentatively employed-for the purpose of buying ammunition, had got into communication with the largest manufacturers of ammunition, and this gentleman had practically, if not absolutely, fixed the price at which it could be obtained in large quantities at $25 per thousand rounds.
I thought the hon. gentleman said $26.50 last night?

I corrected that figure this morning, and I will tell my hon. friend how I got the other figures. My statement further was that before the contracts were definitely closed Mr. Allison appeared on the scene in the city of New York, as representing the Canadian and British Governments, that notices were sent out by him to the various manufacturers of ammunition, representing that he was authorized to act on behalf of the Canadian and British Governments, that as a result of his intervention the manufacturers broke the negotiations which were pending for the supply of ammunition at $25 per thousand rounds, and the price to the British Government was raised to the sum of $33 per thousand rounds. Now, it is only fair to say that my information is that the price to be actually paid to the manufacturers, that is, the net price which they would receive clear of Mr. Allison's commission, was raised from $25 to $26.50; and my information is that that left $6.50 per thousand rounds which would be available for commission to Mr. Allison and his associates, who devoted so much ability, as my hon. friend says, and so much energy in the arranging of these contracts with the manufacturers.

The hon. gentleman has missed his calling; he should have been a professor of mathematics. I enlightened him last night or sought to enlighten him on the figures. When the hon. member in his own Christian spirit and with no desire to do anything but advance the cause of the country first placed the statement on Hansard which he has now given to the Committee, I was not in my place in the House. But I took occasion to look the matter up, and I found that a firm by the name of Flint & Company-I am talking right by the card and I can talk a great deal more if I want to-and the company at Cincinnati held the price up first to $42.50. They then came down to $37.50. This same firm of Flint & Co. claimed to have been instrumental in securing for some American concern a contract with the British Government for 20,000,000 rounds for mark vi ammunition, which I am free to say was at $26.50 per thousand very, very dear, and I venture to say there was quite a rake-off for Flint & Co. if they were instrumental in securing that contract. I understand on inquiry that the Remington Company claim that they secured the contract through the British agent in New York. I do not know who he is, but I understand he is connected with the British Embassy. I understand that they secured this contract through that officer, and that Flint & Company claim that they had something to do with it and have an action pending.* I do not know anything about the merits or demerits of the case, and I care less. But what I do know is that Colonel Wesley Allison has nothing either directly or indirectly to do with that contract.

Is he a real colonel or
an honorary colonel?

He is a real
live wire.
He must be; we will all admit that.
My hon. friend is making out a very bad case for himself.
I am not making out a case at all.

not as expensive an ammunition as our Mark vii.

Because this Mark vii is a British number. The American ammunition is not .so expensive as what is known as -303 Mark vii. The British ammunition costs more, and yet the. American Government; before the war commenced, before the price had gone up, before kupfer nickel had become expensive, before aluminum and lead were in demand, and before powder had got dearer, were being asked $35.76 for this American ammunition. The hon. gentleman .has not the -slightest particle of evidence that there i,s a tittle of fact in what he has stated, and he canno-t produce any. I say so.

Yes, I do know it.

There are some very remarkable stories floating around Canada as to the efficiency, or lack of efficiency, of his engineer service, taking it as a whole. Last August the minister was confronted with an extraordinary condition of affairs, when it was necessary to assemble an army of thirty odd thousand men for overseas service, and he had to as' semble them at a certain point. Every one admits that the minister was wise in his choice of location at Valcartier. So many people in Canada, however, have been there and knew what was going on, that I wish to recall to my hon. friends many of the stories. One is that absolute chaos reigned sppreme in getting ready for the work down at Valcartier, and that my hon. friend's engineer service absolutely fell to pieces. The fact was that so serious did the condition become, my hon. friend was compelled to call upon a rank outsider, a man who up to that date was known as Bob Low, but who since then has been designated by the more euphonious title of Colonel Robert Low. In the Maritime Provinces Bob Low is known as a good contractor. When the engineer service broke down at Valcartier, my hon. friend sent a telegram to Bob Low -I beg his pardon; I mean Colonel Robert Low-asking him if he could send a crew of
300 men down immediately. Bob Low replied,
" If you will send a special train, I will get there." I believe he got there with his men within two or three hours, and set to work and restored order out of chaos. For the work that he performed he was made an honorary colonel, although many men have been made colonels for far less cause than Low was. Low should have been a real colonel, not an honorary colonel. He siiouid have had some real distinction. If I am wrong and Colonel Low did not perform the service, then possibly I am doing an injustice to the engineer corps; but I would like a statement from the minister, and I think it is due to the House and the country for him to state exactly whether the splendid results achieved at Valcartier later on were due to the energy and ability of Colone' Low, or if they were due to the energy and ability of the ordinary engineer services, for which we have been paying such a large amount of money during the past year.

I would point out to my hon. friend that when the war broke out there was no chaos in the Department of Militia and Defence. We got our feet on the table so that the intellects would run down, and in less than twenty-four hours things were moving. On the eighth of August the first day after the division was accepted our engineer forces were on Valcartier ground. The engineers were there: Major Deroche; Major Hughes- not of my clan, but an able man, one of the ablest in Canada; Colonel Maunsell, and other engineers. Colonel Low, who had been manager of the works at the Connaught ranges under Messrs Bate and MacMahon, was an estimable contractor. I invited him down because I knew he had two or three of the best machines for trenching to be found in America, and I knew he was the kind of a man who knew how to drive work ahead. Major Deroche did the engineering work and Colonel Low did the contracting, and it was mighty well done. Three and a half miles of rifle ranges were constructed in ten days. Mr. William Price of Quebec-now Sir William Price-and Mr. COMMONS
McCarthy, a very estimable engineering officer, undertook the laying of the water-mains and twelve miles of water-mains were laid under their direction -

No, by these
gentlemen. When Colonel Low was through with the rifle ranges, having an excellent staff of men, he was good enough to lend . his assistance in other works around the camp. The engineering officers built bridges across the river and they laid out and built roads. A great deal of other w'ork was done that it is not necessary to mention. Whatever opinion I had of my engineering service, before Valcartier, it was changed entirely, and I was surprised and more than delighted to see the splendid energy they displayed, the work they did and the service they gave to the country in this emergency. In the city at present are a large number of engineers, including some hundreds of graduates of the universities of the country standing in the ranks as privates and preparing to go to the front to do their duty there. The engineering service of the Dominion, whatever other department may have fallen down in this emergency, have come splendidly to the front.
Then I take it that Col-oriel Low is not entitled to all the credit given to him in some quarters-
I have never grudged him any credit. He is one of the most energetic, progressive and forceful contractors it has ever been my privilege to meet.

It was .not. I accept the full responsibility. I climbed the hills at Quebec with the object in view of . finding a site for a camp. I felt
10 p.m. that this emergency was going to arise in the near future, and that in any case the district of Quebec required a camp ground for manoeuvering purposes. Then if war ever came-as we hoped then it would not-we would have a training ground in the vicinity of Quebec. But the war did come, and we were so far prepared to meet the emergency. The worst part of the road, however, is that section from the top of the hill to the oamp ground, and I suggest that any permanent work that is propoised should be done to that part of the road. Nothing has been done for some time, but something will have to be done during the present summer. I do not want to press this matter unduly, but, as the minister knows, I have taken ia good deal of interest in this piece of road, and I should like to know if it is the intention of the department to make either temporary or permanent repairs or improvements to the Toad during the coming summer.

The hon. gentleman has brought this matter up on *several occasions, and I must say that his ideas are very practical. A year or two ago we considered the advisability of building a sidewalk up to the Banriefield camp. The hon. member drew our attention to the fact that iit would be better to improve the roadw.ay than to build the sidewalk, and he secured estimates to show that wo could improve the road with the same expenditure as that which was proposed to be made on the construction of
sidewalk. The matter i.s now before our engineering department, and I may say that if we cannot expend the whole amount necessary to complete the roadway this .summer, we certainly will repair it, because our engineers report that it is badly in need of repairs.
Militia and	Defence-permanent	force,
What proportion of the permanent force is now in Bermuda ?
Will the minister give at the same time the present location of the different parts of the entire permanent Canadian force ?

The Royal
Canadian Horse Artillery, the Royal Canadian Dragoons and the Strathcona Horse are, as the hon. member knows, at the front with the engineers and medical corps. We have still a permanent corps, infantry and artillery at Esquimalt. We have permanent forces also at Winnipeg, London, Toronto, Kingston, Quebec and Halifax. The regular Royal Canadian Regiment is at Bermuda.
The Royal Canadian regiment now at Bermuda is a part of the Canadian permanent force?

Yes.
Mr, CARVELL:	Can the minister give
approximately the strength of the respective forces?

I could not
give the exact figures. We are removing some of these troops, but I prefer not to give their destination.

I realize the importance of not divulging military secrets; I am not asking the minister to do that. All the permanent forces that left the country are being paid out of the war vote; there must be but a small proportion of the permanent forces in Canada as compared with a year ago.
No.

The minister can give
us the facts. That is why I wish to get the approximatae strength of the present permanent force.

I will get particulars for the hon. gentleman. For instance, at Kingston, although the Royal Canadian Horse Artillery have gone to the front, the depot is still there. As soon as

the troops are taken away an effort is made to recruit the force up to full strength. At Halifax we are calling out four companies to replace the men who have gone to the front.
Do I understand that when the Royal Canadian Regiment left Halifax for Bermuda the department immediately took steps to recruit a new permanent regiment to be stationed at Halifax?
Yes.

The permanent troops
are paid out of the war credit vote?

Only those
who go to the front.

Take those who have
gone to Bermuda.
That is without the three-mile limit.

That is the Royal Horse Artillery, the Dragoons and the Royal Canadian regiment. That would be a pretty formidable force of men. They are paid out of the special war vote. I know a number of infantry men who were recruited in the Maritime Provinces and taken to Halifax afteP the Royal Canadian regiment was sent to Bermuda. I do not know their exact status; I never understood whether they became a portion of the regulars or permanent force. Would the minister tell whether they are paid out of the war vote or this vote?

These are the troops who are paid out of this vote. They are to replace the men who have gone to the front. Vve are now calling in four new companies from the Maritime Provinces for this permanent regiment.

I have sometimes in the past criticised militia expenditures and I have not much regret for having done so. The thing that has surprised me in the whole conduct of the war by the minister is the fact that we have been spending $JS,0o0,000, or $3,000,000 on a permanent force annually and wnen trouble came the men who were really trained, if there were any in Canada, the men on whom a very large amount had been expended year by year, were not sent to He H0n+ but were sent off to spend the winter in the beautiful climate of Bermuda. This is a remarkable thing and calls for explanation, i do not ask the minister to - uvulge any military secrets.
I am glad the hon. member has brought this matter up, as it gives me an opportunity to meet certain charges, the only 'narges that have been made against me.

I am not making
charges.
Major general HUGHES:	I have been
charged with being unfriendly to the permanent corps. What I have done is to see that the permanent corps get no favour over the militia corps. We are all tne active militia of Canada. But when the war broke out it was my uesire that the Royal Canadian regiment should not go to the front as a unit but that some of the noncommissioned officers and certain of the officers of this corps should be distributed among the other regiments in order to give them the benefit of their training, because these are simply instructional corps. However, about this time the British Government-there is no harm in saying it- requested that we should send the Royal Canadian regiment to Bermuda and release the Lincolnshire regiment then garrisoning Bermuda. We got the order, we recruited tne regiment up to full strength by the addition of 400 or 500 men, and in four days that regiment was sailing for Bermuda, a feat of which my officers are very proud. They are there yet. If the British Government want them at the front all they have to do is to ask them to go to the front and I am sure the Government of Canada would be only too pleased to accede to the request. From time to time personally and against the judgment of the regularly trained officers of the department I have been endeavouring to pick out some of these good fellows from that regiment and send them with the other regiments; but the officers of the department think tnat the regiment should be kept intact as a body and that if they go to the front they should go as the Royal Canadian regiment.
Could the minister explain the retirement of Colonel Alexander Roy, of Victoria?

He has been
retired on leave, getting full pension. I understand that his retirement was perfectly agreeable to him.
Would the minister give some information as to the status of the so-called home guards?

They are
purely voluntary organizations, splendid

organizations, showing the patriotism and loyalty of the Canadian people.

They have such
a company in Toronto, have they not?

They have, I am very glad to say, a company in Toronto.
I had the honour of reviewing them a couple of nights after a certain event.
Interviewing.

I was interviewed first and then I reviewed them and I had the honour of having 20,000 people wait until five minutes to eleven in order that I might review them. They have since formed one of the best regiments in Canada. They had no uniforms last Thursday morning, but on Saturday they marched through the streets of the city in full uniform. The home guard as such are not a part of the militia force, they do not come under the Act. We give them our blessing and wherever we can we lend them some old rifles and furnish targets and ammunition and that sort of thing. That, is all we can afford to give them, they are not under the Militia Department at all.
Are they sworn in as volunteers?

We do not
swear them.
They have their ranks have they not?
Yes. If my hon. friend or any one wishes to call himself a colonel or a major, there is nothing in the law to prevent it.
I was not sura about that.

I know tney do ail over. So does the Salvation Army. In order to meet the desire of these home corps all over the country, and very many of them are ex-milit.ia men and officers, we are bringing them under our Reserve Act. Colonel Mason of the Senate has taken a very active part, with Colonel. Geo. Starke, of Montreal, and others, in organizing this reserve. We are now bringing them under the Reserve Act in connection with the militia and while we cannot do very much for the home guard this will give them a sort of status without expense to the public.
They purchase their own rifles?

I have heard they have purchased some very excellent rifles and in some places corporations have purchased rifles and do not know what to do with them.
Mr. iC. A. WILSON: Is Lieut. Col. Ar-inand Lavergne in the active militia or is he commanding a home guard or has he gone to the front or is he still attorney to the hon. the minister?
Armand Lavergne is colonel of the 61st Montmagny regiment, a very excellent ' regiment-a handsome and excellent colonel.
Is he at the front?
No.
Did he offer his services to the Minister of Militia?
He would not offer them to me, he would offer through the regular channel; he is a well posted officer.

I read in Le Soleil, of Quebec, an article reproduced from Maclean's Magazine saying that the transport of the troops had been delayed for a month because a lady had informed the Minister of Militia that a German Zeppelin was in the Laurentian mountains and the hon. the minister wanted to make an investigation before the troops departed from Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: What is the lady's name?

The article did not mention it, but it said that she met the minister at the table in the Chateau Frontenac and made an appointment for nine in the evening on the corner of Dufferin terrace, that the meeting took place and the lady informed the minister that a German Zeppelin was hovering over the Laurentian mountains, and that consequently it would be unsafe for the troops to embark.

I presume the hon. member saw the lady's picture in the paper. She was a very handsome lady, too. But to my mind the picture of the Minister of Militia did not do him justice, but of course my being nervous and bashful in the presence of the lady might account for that glum look they gave me. The hon. gentleman will see at a glance that it would never do to give away these state secrets.
Does the department furnish rifles to home guards?
No. In one or two places where there were ten or fifteen old rifles I understand that the quartermaster general allowed these associations to make use of them.

The reason I asked was because I have received a communication from a gentleman in my home town who is trying to form a home guard. He said that he had been unable to get rifles, but wished to continue the organization, and I thought perhaps the department might supply them.
I am sorry we are not able to furnish these. What town does my hon. friend refer to.
Sackville.
Will the minister's answer be the same with regard to the home guard of Montreal?
The home guard of Montreal is well armed, they have splendid rifles.
Is the permanent force at Halifax in the same barracks, in many cases, as the contingents?
No, the permanent force is in the Wellington barracks.
Can the minister give us an idea as to the number of volunteer organizations that have been formed since the outbreak of war? I know one has been created in Montreal.
The hon. member does not mean contingents for overseas, but organizations for militia purposes?
The new volunteer organizations that have been authorized. There is talk of forming one in my own constituency, and that is why I am interested.

There is one
in Toronto, two in Montreal, one in Hull; I do not recall any more. I shall be very glad for the Government and the House to support the organization of a regiment in the county of the hon. gentleman. I imagine that the two counties, Gaspe and Bonaventure, could together form one battalion. Amherst has an organization. I should also like to see city regiments in Sydney and Moncton. We have had these plans on hand for some time, but have not been able to prosecute them on account of the cost.
Is the strength of the Canadian permanent force greater today than before the war?

I have not the exact figures, but I think the permanent force is slightly greater. The Royal Canadian Regiment is now kept up to full strength, and in fact nearly all the corps, whereas in times of peace they were not.

I should like to ask a question about cadet corps. A good many towns in Canada are largely interested in these corps, which include the younger boys in a great many families. Many of these companies have been complimented by the commanding officers as being more efficient in drill than the regular companies. The cadet corps of course have nothing to do with the Boy Scouts; they are two different things altogether. Could the minister tell us how many cadets we have in these corps, and whether any have supplied volunteers for the front and, if so, how many? I take a great interest in these cadet corps. I think they are splendid organizations.

I agree with my hon. friend thoroughly. I was very reluctant to reduce the vote for this purpose, but we felt that we should cut down a little the amount for the junior cadets this year, although we have an item in the Supplementary Estimates to keep things going.
I think the cadet corps is one of the most important factors in our militia force. I understand that about 100 boys who have been trained in cadet corps have gone to the front with the Seaforth Highlanders of Vancouver and Victoria, and at the front there will be about ten to fifteen thousand boys who, within the last three years, have trained as cadets. A good proportion of the officers relatively are from the ranks of these associations, and they make excellent officers. I remember seeing a bunch of young lads at Salisbury Plains standing off from the headquarters. I went over to them, ten or fifteen bright, handsome fellows from the Mount St. Louis Institute in Montreal, ' and no regular soldier ever handled himself better than these boys when they marched around the field, and the oflacer said they were just as good in drill. A good many cadets have gone to the front with the Highlanders of Montreal and Vancouver, and a good many from St. Catharines. I have been more than proud to see the splendid results of the cadet training in the boys actually going to the front.

I am glad to hear of that. In the casualty list a day or two ago, were the names of two boys from Renfrew and one

of them, perhaps both, had previously been in the cadet corps in that city. Then in the casualty list published last night was the name of a young man now of Montreal, but formerly of Brockville, and I think he first trained in the Brockville cadet corps. My hon. friend from Brockville (Mr. Webster) and myself are both great friends of his father. This young man went with the Highlanders from Montreal.

Before this item carries I want to place on Hansard a few remarks which I am sure will be agreeably received by members on both sides of the House. I may be excused for doing it, inasmuch as the Royal Military College is situated in a portion of the country which I have the honour to represent. I want to call the attention of the committee to the splendid service which* these cadets have given to the country, and the fine spirit they have manifested since this war broke out. In June, 1914, at the close of the college session, 38 cadets graduated from the Royal Military College, and of these two took imperial commissions, two took commissions in the Canadian permanent force, and all of the remainder of the class of graduates entered units of the Canadian militia, and are now on active service either in Canada or abroad. On the outbreak of the war, on the 4th August last, the War Office offered twenty imperial commissions to Royal Military College cadets, and those to whom the commissions were given were selected from the class which had recently graduated and the senior class expected back in September of that year. The twenty commissions were eagerly accepted I might almost say they were quarrelled over, so eager were the cadets who offered themselves for service. These cadets were gazetted to their positions on September 16, 1914. When the Royal Military College opened on the 1st September last, practically every cadet wanted to go to the war, and it was very difficult to make a selection without hurting the feelings of those who would necessarily be left behind. Many of the students who are at the college for the first time wanted to go, but having had no previous military training, this was out of the question. An army class was formed, and was conducted from the 1st September until the Christmas vacation, and the following cadets received commissions, namely: Imperial army, 49, including the 20 that I have already mentioned; Canadian permanent force, 29; oversea contingents, 25, or a total of 103.
