Every member of this House is interested in the Royal Military College because every province is represented, and worthily represented, by students attending that institution. There are in the Imperial Army list the names of Tegiments which have become famous in the past, and I venture to say that their fame will not be lessened, but will be enhanced because of the addition to their ranks of the cadets of the Royal Military College. We know that since the war broke out several students of the Royal Military College who have gone to the front have distinguished themselves by their valour, and have shed added lustre upon the regiments with which they have become identified. Of all the cadets who were eligible for commissions on the 1st September, 1914, 66 volunteered and were accepted. That represented 77.6 per cent of the attendance at the college, and it is only fair to those who make up the other percentage to say that if they were not included in the 77.6 per cent every one of them wished to join and would have liked to have gone but for various family or other reasons they could not do so. Very many of these obstacles have been removed and the acting commandant of the Royal Military College assures me that fully

50 per cent of the remainder bf the students will likely obtain commissions at the end of the current term.
The attendance at the Royal Military College is restricted. That, I presume, is on account of the accommodation. Only a certain number of pupils can be taken by the college in any one year, hut at the first of this present year they took in 28 additional students in order to fill up the vacancies created by those who have gone to the war. There are 88 cadets in attendance at the college and every one would like to go to the war. The War Office places certain restrictions upon them. They must be of a certain age and they must have been at the college for a certain length of time before they will be allowed to go. I want to pay a tribute to the acting commandant of the Military College at the present time.
Name.

Lt.-Col. Perreau. He has taken a very deep interest in the students and in the welfare of the college, and the results of his work are seen in the rapid progress which the students are making in their studies. I want to pay a tribute to the gentleman who was the commandant of the college immediately preceding Lt.-Col. Perreau. I refer to Col. Carleton. It was a decided acquisition when his services were obtained for the Royal Military College. No finer - gentleman ever set foot in the Dominion of Canada. It was a decided loss to the college when he was requested to go overseas and accept another position in connection with the present war. I hope the time will come when he may return to Canada as commandant of the college. He did much for the college in the short time he was there. As I have said, -every part of Canada is entitled to feel proud because of w-hat has been, -and is being, done -at the Royal Military College, because its students are drawn from every province in Canada and they are reflecting credit on all the provinces from which they come, as well as the college they are attending. We have reason to be proud of the Royal Military College -and its past record, and we have every Tea-son to look forward to its record in the future.
Right here I want to -say a word. I have visited the college, in connection with which there are several buildings, and I must -say that I do not think the classrooms at the present time are what they should be. The students are packed -almost-I was going to say 'like sardines in a box. hut not quite -so closely as that-* 96
but the accommodation is entirely inadequate. If any hon. gentleman wants corroboration of that, I would like him, whenever he is in Kingston, to go over and visit the college for himself, and if he does I am sure he will agree with what I say. Additional dormitories have been provided and that is a move in the right direction. We have a good class of professors, everybody in Canada is proud of the college and its past record, and is desirous of keeping up that record, and the teaching staff -and students -should be encouraged by giving them proper classroom accommodation. I do not know whether there is any portion of this vote that is to he set aside for this purpose or not, but 1 do say that, 'at the earliest possible moment, the buildings where the classrooms are located ought to thoroughly renovated and the students given the -accommodation which they are entitled to. There is every reason why this should be done. The Royal Military -College has been called the " West Point of Canada." It is the only military college we have in Canada, every part of Canada is interested in the obllege and its work, -and I am -sure it is interested in the accommodation of the college and the -appearance of the buildings and grounds. That is partly the reason why I have -advocated very strongly with the present Government, as I did with the past Government, that the -roads around, and in the vicinity of, the college, should be fixed up and put in proper condition, so that people who visit that part of the country will -not have to pass through mud holes in going to or coming from the college. Any person, especially from the United States, or a foreign country, visiting Kingston, invariably crosses over the bridge and visits the college, because it is the only military college we have in the country.
If they pass over good roads and through fine grounds, it is something to our credit. If they pass through mud-holes and over grounds indifferently kept, it is to the discredit not only of that part of the country, but of the whole of Canada, because we are all interested in that college, no matter from what part of Canada we come. I hope the minister and the officials of his department will give this matter of increased accommodation in the class-rooms their serious and earnest attention. I am not desirous of seeing any money thrown away; but I feel proud of the fact that that college is in a corner of my county. I am proud of the work it has done in the past and of the work



it is doing, and I am sure thosehon. members who have visited the place and who have listened to the record that I have placed upon Hansard, will agree with me that the college ought at least to receive every possible consideration at our hands.

I agree with
every word that has fallen from the lips of the hon. member. I am sorry that the condition of finances at the present time does not justify us in placing in the Estimates a sum to meet the requirements as set forth by the hon.. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards). I fully appreciate all that he has said regarding the splendid service of those [DOT] young cadets and of the graduates. Not only from the present classes, but from the classes of by-gone days, they have turned out in splendid numbers. Among the lists of officers, not only in the Imperial service, but in our Canadian service, are to be found scores upon scores of those splendid young fellows. Already I can recall two who have given their lives for the Empire, young Denison and young Ellis, both splendid lads who graduated from that college.
And Carr-Harris.

Yes. I regret that we are not in a position to give what that college really needs, that is a new set of class-rooms, because the present ones are entirely inadequate. I join most heartily in the words of eulogy that have been uttered regarding Lieut.-Col. Perreau, the commanding officer. Those who know him will give him every credit. He deserves a great deal of credit because he is a young officer of distinction who was most anxious to go to the front and who, if he had done so, and if he had come through safely, would have risen very high in the Imperial service for his magnificent conduct in action. This young officer was left in charge, and he has fully justified the confidence placed in him. I am sure I am voicing the sentiments of all who know that institution.

There is considerable feeling in Prince Eupert in regard to the disbandment of the corps that existed there. I think it was drawn to the attention of the minister last year. A further complication arose during the present year. The department wired to the Commanding Officer of the original corps in regard to recruiting. The facts, as they have been submitted to me, are that this corps existed
fMr. Edwards.]
at Prince Rupert, known as the Earl Grey's Own Rifles. The authority to organize the corps was given in 1910. It is represented that at the inspection of 1913, after four annual inspections by four different inspecting officers who commended the offi ers very highly, the District Commanding Officer said that he was going to recommend to Ottawa that the corps be reorganized as a four-company city corps. The department at Ottawa acted on the advice of the District Officer Commanding, and were proceeding to carry out that idea. Letters of instruction to that end were given to the Commanding Officer of the Earl Grey's Own Rifles, and there was considerable enthusiasm over the organization ' and extension of the corps; but there were apparently some local reasons from some envious sources that caused some questions to arise-that is as the case is represented to me-and an Order was sent from Ottawa disbanding the corps.. On the disbandment of the corps, a public meeting was held to denounce the action of the local parties who, it was alleged, had made the representations. After the corps had been broken up and the arms and equipment sent back to Victoria, war broke out. A Fusilier corps was sent to protect the city, and they are still on the job. Then an attempt was made to reorganize the regiment. That went on during the late autumn. The consequence was that, by reason of the disbandment of the corps known as the Earl Grey's Own Rifles and the confusion that was occasioned thereby, the military interest in the community was considerably disorganized and a great deal of feeling resulted. I would like the minister to state his views in regard to this matter and say whether the representations that have been made to me are correct or not.

There was some difficulty in connection with the organization in Prince Rupert some two or three years ago. VI will not enter into the details of the causes, because I have heard them set forth by my hon. friend at different times. I cannot pretend to solve the difficulty by repeating them. There is nothing to be hidden so far as I am connected with the matter. It was, I think, a one-company corps and it was disbanded for the purpose of reorganization. My recollection is that it was re-organized, because while I was looking at the troops at Victoria, I met a number of the officers both in the Victoria regiment and in the Vancouver regiment who came from that corps.

I remember two or three of the leading officers. I think the matter is pretty well settled now, and that they are all doing their duty. If the hon. member wishes me to look up the matter, I will do so and bring down the information to-morrow.

Here is a letter published in 1914, a year ago:
T have the honour, hy direction, to inform you that a general order authorizing the disbandment of Earl Grey's Own Rifles with a view to re-organization as a four-company city corps will be issued shortly. The present officers of this corps will be placed on the reserve of officers.
It is complained by those men, who were in the Earl Grey's Own Rifles, and who gave considerable energy and enthusiasm to the success of that organization, that they were not placed on the reserve of officers; that they are not now on the reserve, and that they were completely and absolutely disregarded.

Might I point out to the hon. member that it is the usual custom, when a regiment is disbanded for re-organization to place the officers on the reserve. Otherwise they would be put out entirely. It is only a temporary step. Then those who choose to come in can come into the new organization. The matter is fairly well settled now.

That is not the representation that has been made to me. Here is a letter written under date of February 19, 1914:	,
In reference to your letter of February 10th advising me of the proposed disbandment, of Earl Grey's Own R fies, and also in regard to your general order of February 12th respecting recommendations submitted to headquarters for the retirement or removal of officers from Canadian milita, I beg to say that Lieutenant McMordie, Lieutenant Agnew and myself have no desire to be removed from the active militia. I hold a field officer's certificate issued in 1907, No. 12811, and Lieut. McMordie holds a cap-ta'n's certificate, April 15, 1912, No. 2343.
I would be pleased to be informed as to why these removals are being made and upon which officer's recommendation these changes are being considered.
I know of no cause or reason for this being done.
I have the honour to be, sir,
Your obedient servant,
Alfred Stork,
Capt. E.G.O.R.
He alleges that to that letter no reply was received.

To whom was it addressed?
96*

The District Officer
Commanding Military District No. 11, Victoria. Then on the 29th of April:
Instructions have been received this day from Ottawa per the District Staff Adjutant M.D. No. XI, for the withdrawal of all arms, ammunition, clothing and equipment from the unit under your command.
Will you therefore kindly return all stores to the Ordnance Officer M.D. No. XI, Esquimau, B.C., and mark all cases " Freight colJ lect."
Please give this matter your early attention.
This was done. It is asserted that the disorganization of the military conditions in Prince Rupert, the disbandment of the Earl Grey Rifles, and the 'displacement of the men who had taken an interest in this matter and had done a great deal in military work, was due to representations of local politicians and not to any desire to further the militia interest of the district. The minister intimates that something has been done in regard to the matter. I happened to meet Captain Stork who I know personally-
Is that the gentleman who went to the front?
I do not know. This information came to me over a month ago and did not come direct from him. It is claimed that discrimination was shown in regard to the acceptance of men in the district.

I remember that when the first contingent was organized the Prince Rupert people were not called on. The officers at the coast did
11 p.m. not accept the contingent from Prince Rupert; they said they felt that that small community required all the men that could be mustered there to prevent raiding. And I understand they had to be supplemented by soldiers from Vancouver, the Fusiliers. But when the second contingent was sent-'the hon. gentleman, no doubt, saw them while in Ottawa-there were, I think, 300 men from Prince Rupert. I know there were a number of officers, because I spoke to them and congratulated them on their splendid appearance. I understood that whatever little friction there had been at first had all been overcome when the war began, that the boys forgot their local differences in the great issue before the country.

The peculiar thing is that these instructions were sent to Victoria

after the company was disbanded and before the efforts made at reorganization. Under these instructions Captain Stork was to enlist men. He had enlisted about a hundred when instructions came to him to stop, throwing the whole work into confusion.
I think that this was because of fear of a raid.
But the recruiting was taken from him and placed in the hands of another party.

I have no record of that. It came from Victoria. Of course, I do not carry all these things in my mind. If the hon. gentleman wants the facts and will come to the office we will be. glad to give them.
I can hardly go there and be at the committee investigating the purchase of boots at the same time.
I am at the office at eight o'clock, and shall be glad to see him then.

The hon. gentleman is too generous. As to the number of men who were under arms in British Columbia in various military services, I may say that there seemed to be a great need of men. Something like 4,000 men were kept under arms, not for the purpose of going to the front but for local purposes. And they were so kept under arms for quite a long time. I would like to get the exact cost.
And to what account it was charged.

We will try to get that. The hon. member will understand that British Columbia is an isolated province, and that it controls our greatest highway. One charge of dynamite properly placed and set off might prevent the crossing of any train from coast to coast for three months. At the time when there was a talk of trouble between the Japanese and the United States people, the United States Government wakened up to realize that every bridge along their transcontinental lines, every pass and tunnel, could be blown up, and probably would be blown up, if trouble should arise. They realized that it would take them at least nine months to repair these bridges, passes and tunnels so that one train could cross. Realizing that the railway through the mountains is in this regard a national asset, we have been guarding it through the mountains and at all exposed points along
l-Mr. MavdonMct]
the way. Then, as to the soldiers at Prince Rupert, all these isolated and important points, Esquimalt, Halifax, Victoria, had to be guarded, especially when fear existed of activity of submarines.
Was the cost of maintaining these men and services part of the war debt, or was it charged to local militia charges?
It is part of the war debt.
Would the minister be good enough to bring down a statement of the number of men and the cost?
I am not sure that we have the figures of cost, but the numbers are given. However, we will endeavour to get the information.

The minister^ offer to receive me at his office in the early morning is a seductive proposition, but I am afraid I can hardly intimate to him that I can accept it in these strenuous days.
Militia and Defence-schools of instruction, $140,000.
Where are these schools?

In the large
local centres we have provisional schools of instruction as well as regular schools. In almost every large town in the countrj we have schools for training officers. There are also schools in connection with the universities.
They pass the examinations at the local schools?

Yes. They
have what is called a war class at the Royal Military College now.

Will the minister tell the
committee what arrangements have been made with colleges with regard to military training? I refer particularly to Mount Allison University.

Nearly all universities in the country have formed what we call an officers' training corps. I should be glad to send the printed particulars to my hon. friend. Sackville already has one; they have a splendid cadet corps.

I understand that a gentleman by the name of Borden-a military official at Halifax; I do not know his title- is coming to Mount Allison to give military instruction to the students. I understand also that the Government has paid a cer-

tain amount for fixing up a building there for training purposes.
We are furnishing instructors; I do' not know whether or not we fitted up a hall. I will look into the matter.

Will the minister
give the committee some information with regard to a special corps that is being organized, under the auspices, I think, of the Canadian Pacific Railway? I have a telegram here from three boys in my county who want to volunteer for enlistment in this corps, but who do not know how to go about it.	[DOT]

The corps is
being organized under the leadership of Colonel Ramsey, chief engineer of the Canadian Pacific Railway. I think the corps is to consist of 500 men. Applications may be sent to Colonel Ramsey at Montreal.
What is the title of the corps?

speechtext:
It is a railway
engineering corps, I think.

Applications
may be addressed to Col. Ramsey of the Overseas Railway Engineering Corps. Inasmuch as I suggest that the boys may send their applications to the hon. member for Pictou, who can forward them to Col. Ramsey.	, . ,

What is the corps which
is being organized by Mr. Janin, former city engineer of Montreal?

That is an engineering corps; they may be seen at any time at the exhibition grounds. We mobilized a brigade of artillery some weeks ago. Some hon. gentlemen had the privilege of seeing them in front of the buildings this afternoon. One company section of about 80 men was made up of third and fourth year men from the University of Toronto. A finer lot of soldiers it would be hard to find; their marching was almost equal to that of the old regulars, although they have been organized only three weeks. I suggest to all hon. gentlemen that they pay the boys a visit; it would be a source of great pleasure and inspiration to them.
Have the companies from McGill University gone to the front?

Some have
gone, others will go.

I was informed last night that Col. Ramsey had not obtained his full
complement of men for the engineering corps of the Canadian Pacific Railway. Some of these young men have had experience in railway engineering work, and from what I heard from a Canadian Pacific Railway man last night, Col. Ramsey is going to have a magnificent corps. The minister has to be in his office at eight o' clock in the morning, and in order that he may be good-natured when he gets there I suggest that we pass item 96 and leave 97 and 98-in respect of these some hon. gentlemen wish to make comment or to ask questions-and then adjourn.
All right.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I agree with
what the hon. member for South Renfrew said about the engineering corps; I think it is going to be a very fine corps. I may say, in addition to the explanation given by the Minister of Militia-I know something of this, having been Acting Minister for a time-that it was suggested from this side in October Tast that we have in Canada a number of very capable railway engineers and railway contractors, men accustomed to doing things quickly, whose services might be very valuable indeed in connection with the rebuilding of railways that had been destroyed in the course of the war. At that time it was not thought that they were needed, but later-I think it was in February-we received an intimation from the War Office that they would be very glad if such a corps could be organized in Canada. We got in touch with some of the large railway corporations, and eventually it was left to Colonel Ramsey who, I understand, is a very capable man, to undertake the organization of this corps. It was thought that by reason of his knowledge and experience he would be able to do this work more effectively than if it were done by the department itself. The matter, therefore, has been left entirely to him, and from what I have heard of the progress which has been made in organizing the corps, it promises to be a most excellent body of men; I have no doubt that they will do excellent work when they get to the front. The Minister of Militia informs me that applications for enlistment in this corps will be received at the office of any divisional superintendent throughout the country.
Progress reported.	.
